name: Microsoft Certified: Information Security Administrator Associate
note: Microsoft scores SC-401 on a 1–1000 scale with 700 to pass. Practice exams here report a straight percentage; treat 80% as your readiness bar.

cs1.title: Case Study — Northwind Traders (Legal Services)
cs1.body:
Northwind Traders is a legal services firm with 1,500 employees on Microsoft 365 E5.

• Client matter numbers stored in a SQL database (format: MATTER-XXXXXX)
• NDA templates and legal briefs stored in SharePoint Online
• Legacy client documents on on-premises Windows file servers
• BYOD iOS and Android devices managed via Microsoft Intune
• External clients and opposing counsel receive confidential legal briefs via email
• Microsoft 365 Copilot deployed for 200 senior attorneys

yn1.title: Yes / No
yn1.body:
Northwind Traders applies two retention labels: Client Matter — Regulatory Record (Regulatory Record type, 7-year period) and Internal Documents (Regular Record type, 3-year period). A sensitivity label Strictly Confidential uses Assign permissions now encryption scoped to senior attorneys only.

For each statement, select Yes if it is true or No if it is false.

cs2.title: Case Study — Adatum Corporation (Pharma Research)
cs2.body:
Adatum Corporation is a pharmaceutical research company with 8,000 employees on Microsoft 365 E5.

• Scanned lab reports (PDF images from flatbed scanners) uploaded to SharePoint Online
• Proprietary drug compound names unique to Adatum — not publicly documented, no consistent alphanumeric pattern
• Most sensitive trade secret documents require encryption that no cloud provider can access
• External academic collaborators have B2B guest accounts in Adatum Teams and SharePoint
• FDA 21 CFR Part 11 compliance required for all electronic records

yn2.title: Yes / No
yn2.body:
Adatum configures the MPIP Scanner on Windows Server 2022 to scan on-premises network shares. A content scan job is created with Policy enforcement set to Off (Discover mode). SQL Server Express is installed on the scanner server.

For each statement, select Yes if it is true or No if it is false.

cs3.title: Case Study — Litware Inc (Technology Company)
cs3.body:
Litware Inc is a technology company with 3,000 employees on Microsoft 365 E5.

• Developer-heavy workforce; GitHub repositories connected to Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps
• SharePoint Online used for project documentation and design specifications
• BYOD allowed for managers — iOS and Android devices enrolled in Microsoft Intune
• Microsoft 365 Copilot deployed for all 200 managers
• GDPR compliance required — EU customer personal data is processed and stored in M365

yn3.title: Yes / No
yn3.body:
Litware has Microsoft 365 E5 licenses. The compliance admin reviews this PowerShell command:

    Search-UnifiedAuditLog -StartDate 05/01/2026 -EndDate 05/20/2026 -RecordType SharePointFileOperation -Operations FileAccessed

Litware also has a 5-year custom SharePoint retention policy and a default 90-day org-wide retention policy applied to the same SharePoint locations.

For each statement, select Yes if it is true or No if it is false.

questions.stem: Northwind must detect documents with the same structural layout as their blank NDA template — without relying on keywords or regex patterns. Which SIT approach should they use?
options: A custom regex SIT matching NDA section headers and terminology
An Exact Data Match (EDM) classifier using NDA field values
A trainable classifier trained on signed NDA examples
A document fingerprint of the blank NDA template file
questions.explanation: D is correct. Document fingerprinting hashes the structural layout of a template — field positions, section ordering, paragraph skeleton — and detects new documents that share the same structure regardless of the data filled in. This is purpose-built for blank forms like NDAs, W-2s, and standardized contracts. A is wrong because regex matches text patterns and the question explicitly rules out keyword/regex approaches. B (EDM) is wrong because EDM compares document content against actual database values, which is useful for matter numbers or SSNs but not for structural similarity. C (trainable classifier) is wrong because classifiers identify content TOPICS from training examples; a classifier trained on signed NDAs would match documents 'about' NDAs broadly but could not reliably isolate Northwind's specific template structure.

questions.stem: Northwind must detect actual client matter numbers from their SQL database to eliminate false positives from similar-looking codes in documents. Which SIT type should they create?
options: A document fingerprint based on a matter intake form template
A named entity SIT for financial matter identifiers
An EDM classifier built from the actual SQL database records
A custom regex SIT with the MATTER-[0-9]{6} pattern and keyword corroboration
questions.explanation: C is correct. EDM hashes the actual matter-number values from Northwind's SQL database and uses those hashes as the match source — so a string only counts as a match if it exists in the source data. This eliminates false positives from unrelated codes that merely look like MATTER-XXXXXX. D is wrong because a regex SIT matches anything fitting the format whether or not the matter number is real — exactly the false-positive problem they need to solve. A is wrong because fingerprinting detects template structure, not specific data values. B is wrong because there is no built-in 'financial matter identifiers' named entity SIT — named entity SITs cover broad categories (person names, addresses, medical terms), not custom internal identifiers.

questions.stem: BYOD users access SharePoint sites containing sensitive legal documents from personal browser sessions. Northwind wants to prevent file downloads and printing from unmanaged (non-Intune) sessions without fully blocking access. What should they configure?
options: A sensitivity label with Assign permissions now encryption on all documents in the site
A conditional access policy requiring Intune compliance before any SharePoint access is permitted
A DLP policy blocking SharePoint downloads on non-Intune-enrolled devices
A container sensitivity label on the SharePoint site configured to allow web-only access for unmanaged devices
questions.explanation: D is correct. Container sensitivity labels on SharePoint sites include an 'Unmanaged devices' setting with three options: block access, allow limited web-only access (view in browser, no download/print/sync), or allow full access. Web-only meets both requirements — users can still read documents but cannot extract them from BYOD devices. The setting leverages Entra ID Conditional Access App Control under the hood but is configured directly on the container label. C is wrong because SharePoint DLP has no device-state condition — DLP inspects content, not device posture; recognizing whether a device is Intune-managed is the job of Conditional Access. A is wrong because file-level encryption applies uniformly to all access regardless of device — it doesn't selectively block download on BYOD while allowing it on corporate endpoints, and it doesn't gate printing differently per device. B is wrong because requiring Intune compliance for ANY SharePoint access fully blocks BYOD usage, contradicting the requirement to allow read access.

questions.stem: Northwind must send legal briefs to external clients via email. The emails must expire after 30 days and must be revocable after sending if the client relationship ends. Which technology provides BOTH capabilities?
options: Microsoft Purview Advanced Message Encryption with expiration date and revocation configured
Standard Office 365 Message Encryption using the Encrypt-Only protection template
S/MIME certificate-based encryption with client-side key management
A sensitivity label with Do Not Forward IRM permissions applied before sending
questions.explanation: A is correct. Advanced Message Encryption (an M365 E5 capability) is the only Microsoft email encryption option that supports BOTH time-based expiration (the message becomes unreadable after a configured date) AND post-send revocation (the sender or admin can revoke access to a message that has already been delivered). D is wrong because Do Not Forward IRM prevents forwarding/printing/copying but cannot expire or revoke. B is wrong because standard OME Encrypt-Only encrypts at send time but has no expiration timer and no revocation. C is wrong because S/MIME relies on certificate-based encryption between endpoints; once the recipient decrypts the message, the sender has no mechanism to expire or revoke it.

questions.stem: Which named entity SIT should you use to detect full person names across diverse European, Asian, and Middle Eastern naming conventions for GDPR subject rights compliance?
options: All Full Names
All Physical Addresses
All Personal Data Identifiers
EU Passport Number
questions.explanation: A (All Full Names) is correct. It is a named entity SIT that uses an ML model trained on multilingual name data to recognize person names across European, Asian, Middle Eastern, and other naming conventions without relying on fixed patterns. B (All Physical Addresses) is wrong because it detects addresses, not names. D (EU Passport Number) is wrong — it is a structured regex SIT for travel document identifiers, not person names. C is wrong because 'All Personal Data Identifiers' is not a named entity SIT in Microsoft Purview — Purview's bundled GDPR SITs have specific names like 'EU Driver's License Number,' 'EU National Identification Number,' or the 'EU GDPR Enhanced' bundle, but none is named 'All Personal Data Identifiers.'

questions.stem: In an Exact Data Match (EDM) sensitive information type, what is the role of the primary element?
options: It specifies the hashing algorithm applied to the database records before upload
It is the main sensitive field the SIT actively searches for in document or email content
It defines which users have permission to view EDM-matched content in DLP reports
It sets the confidence threshold above which EDM results are reported
questions.explanation: B is correct. The primary element is the central sensitive field EDM actively searches for in content — for example, the SSN column in an HR data table. Supporting elements (last name, date of birth) corroborate the match in proximity and raise confidence from medium to high, but the primary element MUST match for any result to fire. A is wrong because the hashing algorithm is fixed by EDM itself and not defined by the primary element. C is wrong because access to EDM-matched content in DLP reports is governed by RBAC roles, not by SIT configuration. D is wrong because confidence thresholds are set on the DLP rule, not embedded in the primary element definition.

questions.stem: A container sensitivity label is applied to a Microsoft Teams team. Which settings does it control?
options: Whether DLP policies apply to chat messages in that specific team
Whether it's private, allows guests, and limits unmanaged devices
Whether Teams meeting recordings are labeled when saved to SharePoint
Whether files in team channels are automatically encrypted when uploaded
questions.explanation: B is correct. Container labels on Teams teams (which also govern the connected M365 Group and SharePoint site) control: privacy (public vs private), external/guest access, and unmanaged-device access. They govern the container itself — not files inside. D is wrong because container labels do NOT automatically encrypt files in channels; file-level encryption is a document-level sensitivity-label setting. C is wrong because Teams meeting recordings are labeled by meeting-scoped or file-scoped sensitivity labels, not by the container label on the team. A is wrong because container labels do not configure DLP scope — DLP policies have their own location targeting and conditions, independent of the team's container label.

questions.stem: What control does Microsoft 365 Customer Key provide that standard Microsoft-managed encryption does NOT?
options: Per-user granular encryption keys scoped to individual mailboxes
Encryption of data flowing between Microsoft datacenter regions
Control over the root keys that protect Microsoft 365 data at rest
End-to-end encryption of emails without requiring Outlook or Microsoft 365
questions.explanation: C is correct. Customer Key (BYOK at the Microsoft 365 service layer) lets the organization supply and control the root keys that wrap Microsoft's data-at-rest encryption keys for Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Teams. By revoking those keys, the organization can render its M365 data unreadable — even to Microsoft. D is wrong because Customer Key does not change message-level end-to-end encryption — it operates at the service storage layer. A is wrong because Customer Key keys are tenant- or DEP-scoped, not per-user mailbox keys. B is wrong because encryption of data in transit between Microsoft datacenter regions is a separate Microsoft platform capability and is not what Customer Key controls.

questions.stem: Highly sensitive documents are protected with Double Key Encryption (DKE). Which trade-off should the organization expect?
options: Protection is removed automatically after 30 days unless it's renewed
The documents can be opened only on devices that run Windows Server
Microsoft 365 services such as search, DLP, and Copilot can't read the content
The documents can't be shared with any user inside the organization's tenant
questions.explanation: Because Microsoft holds only one of the two keys, Microsoft 365 services can't decrypt DKE content to index, inspect, or reason over it — search, eDiscovery review, DLP content inspection, and Copilot don't work on it. That's why DKE is reserved for a small set of the most sensitive content. DKE content opens in Office apps on client devices for authorized users, has no automatic 30-day expiry, and can be shared with authorized internal users.

questions.stem: Unlike Microsoft Purview Message Encryption (OME), what is a distinctive infrastructure requirement for S/MIME to function?
options: S/MIME requires Microsoft Entra ID accounts for both communicating parties
Both sender and recipient must have Microsoft 365 E5 licensing
The recipient must access the message via Outlook on the web to decrypt it
Both parties need X.509 certificates from a trusted authority
questions.explanation: D is correct. S/MIME is built on PKI: both sender and recipient must hold X.509 certificates issued by a trusted CA and installed on their devices/clients. Without those certificates, S/MIME cannot sign or encrypt. B is wrong — S/MIME is not tied to E5 licensing; it ships in Outlook/Exchange. C is wrong because that describes the OME web-portal experience for external recipients, not S/MIME. A is wrong — S/MIME does not require Entra ID accounts on either side; it works between any two parties with valid certificates, including cross-organization.

questions.stem: A label policy has a default label of Internal. A user creates a new Word document and saves it without changing the label. Does this satisfy mandatory labeling?
options: No — mandatory labeling still requires the user to actively confirm the label even when a default is configured
Yes — the default label is automatically applied and fully satisfies the mandatory labeling requirement
Yes, but only if the default label configuration includes encryption
No — the default label is applied but the user must confirm it within 24 hours before sharing
questions.explanation: B is correct. When a sensitivity-label policy is configured with a default label, that label is applied automatically to new content at creation time. Because the document is labeled, mandatory labeling is satisfied without re-prompting the user. A is wrong because no extra user confirmation is required when a default is in effect. D is wrong because there is no 24-hour confirmation grace period. C is wrong because the encryption configuration of the default label is irrelevant to mandatory labeling — what matters is that a label is applied.

questions.stem: What is the minimum number of seed content items required to initiate training of a custom trainable classifier?
options: 25 items
10 items
50 items
200 items
questions.explanation: C (50 items) is correct. Custom trainable classifiers in Microsoft Purview require a minimum of 50 (and up to 500) seed items placed in a dedicated SharePoint folder before training can begin. B (10) and A (25) are wrong because both are below the documented minimum and the classifier will not begin training. D (200) is wrong because, although 200 is within the allowed seed range, the question asks for the MINIMUM — and 200 is far above it.

questions.stem: A label hierarchy has parent label Confidential with sublabel Confidential - Legal. A user selects Confidential - Legal from the sensitivity bar in Word. What is applied to the document?
options: Both Confidential and Confidential - Legal labels are applied simultaneously to the document
Only Confidential - Legal is applied — the parent is implied by the hierarchy but not separately applied
Only the parent label Confidential is applied — sublabel settings inherit into the parent
The user must first apply Confidential and then separately apply the sublabel in a second step
questions.explanation: B is correct. When a user selects a sublabel from the sensitivity bar, only that single sublabel is applied — Office records exactly one sensitivity label per file. The parent provides organization in the menu and may share visual marking/encryption settings, but it is not separately stored on the document. A is wrong because a document carries exactly one label at a time, not both parent and sublabel simultaneously. C is wrong because applying the sublabel does not back-apply the parent — the sublabel itself is what is recorded. D is wrong because no two-step apply workflow exists; selecting the sublabel applies it directly.

questions.stem: A Highly Confidential sensitivity label with encryption is applied to a Power BI semantic model. A user exports the dataset to Excel. What happens to the sensitivity label?
options: The label is removed — Excel manages its own label policy independently
The label and encryption are both transferred to the exported Excel file
The user must manually re-apply the label in Excel after completing the export
The label is applied to the Excel file but encryption is removed for application compatibility
questions.explanation: B is correct. When Power BI semantic models are exported to Office formats (Excel, PowerPoint, PDF), the sensitivity label AND its protection settings — encryption, content marking text, watermarks — flow through to the exported file. This is how Power BI's label-aware export keeps protection attached to data leaving the model. A is wrong because Excel does not maintain a separate label policy; sensitivity labels are tenant-wide. D is wrong because Power BI preserves encryption on export; encryption is not dropped 'for compatibility.' C is wrong because no manual re-application is needed — Power BI handles this automatically.

questions.stem: You want the MPIP Scanner to identify files containing sensitive information on on-premises file shares WITHOUT applying labels or modifying any files. Which scanner configuration achieves this?
options: Deploy the scanner with Policy enforcement set to On (Enforce mode)
Deploy it with Policy enforcement set to Off (Discover mode)
Deploy the scanner in Audit mode with an instance count threshold set to zero
Deploy the scanner with TestWithNotifications mode to preview labeling actions
questions.explanation: B is correct. Setting Policy enforcement = Off on the content scan job puts the MPIP Scanner in Discover (audit-only) mode — it scans, identifies matches, and reports without applying labels or modifying files. This is the recommended validation step before enabling Enforce mode. A is wrong because Enforce mode (Policy enforcement = On) actively applies labels and protection. D is wrong because 'TestWithNotifications' is DLP-policy terminology, not an MPIP Scanner mode — the Scanner's modes are Discover (Off) and Enforce (On). C is wrong because 'Audit mode with instance count threshold zero' is not a Scanner configuration; the Scanner's behavior is governed by the Policy enforcement flag.

questions.stem: Mandatory labeling is enabled in the label policy. No default label is configured. A user composes an email in Outlook and clicks Send without selecting a label. What happens?
options: The email sends with an auto-generated None classification applied
Outlook applies the most recently used label from the user's label history
The email is queued and held for admin review until a label is applied
Outlook blocks sending and prompts the user to select a sensitivity label
questions.explanation: D is correct. With mandatory labeling enabled and no default label, Outlook blocks the Send action and prompts the user to select a sensitivity label before the message can leave the client. A is wrong because there is no 'auto-generated None' classification — mandatory labeling does not invent a placeholder. C is wrong because emails are not queued for admin review; the user is blocked client-side. B is wrong because Outlook does not silently apply a recently used label to satisfy mandatory labeling — the user must make the choice explicitly.

questions.stem: A sensitivity label is configured with Teams meetings scope only. Where is this label available for users to apply?
options: In Teams group chats and one-on-one conversations
In the Teams admin center when managing meeting configuration policies
In Teams channels when creating a new post or announcement
In the meeting options when scheduling or configuring a meeting
questions.explanation: D is correct. Teams meeting-scoped labels surface in meeting scheduling and meeting options (in the Teams calendar and Outlook calendar). They configure lobby rules, who can present, end-to-end encryption requirements, recording permissions, and chat behavior. C is wrong because channel posts are governed by file/site labels and DLP, not meeting labels. A is wrong because chats are not meetings and do not expose meeting labels. B is wrong because the Teams admin center manages tenant Teams settings — sensitivity labels are administered in the Microsoft Purview portal, not the Teams admin center.

questions.stem: An event-based retention label has a 5-year period linked to event type Contract Expiry. The label is applied to a contract on January 1, 2025, but no Contract Expiry event is created. When does the 5-year clock start?
options: January 1, 2025 — when the label is applied to the document
When the contract natural expiry date passes based on the document content
The clock does not start until a Contract Expiry event is created in Microsoft Purview
January 1, 2026 — one year after label application as a default trigger
questions.explanation: C is correct. Event-based retention does not start when the label is applied — it starts only when an event of the matching event type is created in Microsoft Purview (via portal, Graph API, or PowerShell). Until that event is created, the retention clock has not started. A is wrong precisely because label application alone does not start the clock. B is wrong because Purview cannot infer a natural expiry date from document content. D is wrong because there is no automatic 1-year default trigger — the event is the only trigger.

questions.stem: You need to apply a 3-year retention policy to Viva Engage community messages. Which location should you select in the Microsoft Purview retention policy configuration?
options: SharePoint Online — Viva Engage community sites
Viva Engage — community messages
Exchange Online — public folders
Microsoft Teams — channel messages (Viva Engage integrates into Teams)
questions.explanation: B is correct. Viva Engage (formerly Yammer) has dedicated retention locations in Purview: 'Viva Engage community messages' and 'Viva Engage user messages.' These are separate from Teams, Exchange, and SharePoint and must be explicitly selected. D is wrong because Viva Engage is NOT covered by Teams channel retention — it is a separate workload. C is wrong because Viva Engage data is not stored in Exchange public folders. A is wrong because while Viva Engage uses some SharePoint storage under the hood, retention is configured against the Viva Engage location, not the underlying SharePoint sites.

questions.stem: A SharePoint site covered by an active 3-year Microsoft Purview retention policy is deleted by a Site Collection Administrator. What happens to the site content?
options: Content moves to the Site Collection recycle bin for 93 days and is then permanently deleted
Content is preserved in the Preservation Hold Library for the full 3-year retention period despite the site deletion
The site and all content are permanently deleted — site deletion overrides any active retention policies
Content is transferred to a SharePoint archive site created automatically by the retention system
questions.explanation: B is correct. Retention policies survive site deletion. When a site under an active retention policy is deleted, its content is captured in the Preservation Hold Library for the full retention period and remains searchable via eDiscovery — even after the site itself is gone. C is wrong because site deletion does NOT override retention. A is wrong because while the SharePoint recycle bin holds deleted items for 93 days, the retention policy preserves content for the full 3 years beyond the recycle bin. D is wrong because Microsoft does not auto-provision an 'archive site' — the mechanism is the Preservation Hold Library.

questions.stem: When is an Exchange Online mailbox converted to an inactive mailbox rather than being permanently deleted when the user account is removed?
options: When the mailbox size exceeds 50 GB at the time of account deletion
When the mailbox has had no activity for more than 30 days prior to deletion
When a hold or retention policy covers it before the account is deleted
When the organization has Microsoft 365 E5 licensing at the time of account deletion
questions.explanation: C is correct. An inactive mailbox is created automatically when a user account is deleted IF a hold (litigation hold, eDiscovery hold) or a retention policy is in place on the mailbox at deletion time. The hold prevents permanent removal, and Exchange retains the mailbox indefinitely for compliance and eDiscovery. B is wrong because mailbox-activity history is not the determinant. D is wrong because E5 licensing does not automatically convert a mailbox to inactive — the hold/retention policy does. A is wrong because mailbox size has no bearing on inactive-mailbox creation.

questions.stem: Who can be designated as a disposition reviewer for a retention label in Microsoft Purview?
options: eDiscovery Managers with active content search permissions
Any internal user or mail-enabled security group
Global Administrators and Compliance Administrators
Members of the Records Management or Compliance Administrator role groups
questions.explanation: B is correct. Any internal user or mail-enabled security group can be designated as a disposition reviewer in the retention label configuration. There is no special admin-role requirement to BE a reviewer (though managing the disposition workflow itself does require Records Management or equivalent rights). D is wrong because reviewers do not have to be in Records Management or Compliance Administrator. A is wrong because eDiscovery roles do not gate disposition review. C is wrong because Global/Compliance Admin roles are not required for reviewers.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of sequential disposition review stages that can be configured in a single retention label?
options: 5 stages
2 stages
3 stages
10 stages
questions.explanation: A (5 stages) is correct. A single retention label supports up to 5 sequential disposition review stages, each with its own reviewers and time window. After all configured stages complete, the disposition outcome (retain, dispose, relabel) is finalized. B (2) and C (3) are wrong because both are below the documented 5-stage maximum. D (10 stages) is wrong because Microsoft caps stages at 5 — not 10.

questions.stem: A DLP rule is set to Block, but allow business justification override. A user attempts to email a file with 15 credit card numbers externally. What is the user experience?
options: The email is routed to an admin approval queue before delivery to the external recipient
The send action is permanently blocked with no option to proceed
The file credit card numbers are automatically redacted before sending
The user sees a policy tip and can provide a business justification to override and send
questions.explanation: D is correct. Block-with-override shows the user a policy tip explaining the violation and offers a business-justification field. After supplying a justification (and optionally a category/reason), the user can proceed; the override action and justification text are logged in DLP activity reports for compliance review. B is wrong because overrides are explicitly permitted in this configuration. C is wrong because DLP does not auto-redact content — that is not an out-of-the-box DLP action. A is wrong because there is no admin-approval queue in block-with-override; the override is self-service with an audit trail.

questions.stem: Two separate DLP policies target the same Exchange email. Policy A (priority 0): block when credit card count exceeds 10. Policy B (priority 1): notify admin when count exceeds 5. The email contains 12 credit card numbers. What happens?
options: Both policies apply independently — the email is blocked (Policy A) AND an admin notification is sent (Policy B)
Only Policy A fires — higher priority policy suppresses all lower-priority policies for the same item
Only Policy B fires — it has a lower count threshold so it matches first
The email is blocked and no notification is sent — the most restrictive action wins across all policies
questions.explanation: A is correct. When content matches rules in several DLP policies, the most restrictive action (the block from Policy A) is enforced, and incident reports and alerts from every matching rule — including Policy B's admin notification — are still sent. B is wrong because separate policies do not suppress each other based on priority. C is wrong because the lower threshold does not 'win' across policies — both are evaluated. D is wrong because notifications still fire even when a block is in place; the 'most restrictive wins' shortcut does not apply across separate policies.

questions.stem: A Windows 11 device onboarded to MDE is offline with no internet connectivity. Endpoint DLP policies are deployed. What happens to DLP enforcement while offline?
options: DLP enforcement is completely suspended until the device reconnects to the corporate network
The device is isolated by MDE and DLP is bypassed during the offline period by design
Only block actions continue offline — audit and notify actions are paused
DLP policies continue enforcing based on the last synced policy settings cached locally on the device
questions.explanation: D is correct. Endpoint DLP caches the most recently synced policy locally on the device (via MDE). When the device is offline, the cached policy continues to enforce — blocks, audits, and notifications all stay active. New policy changes do not take effect until the device reconnects and syncs. A is wrong because enforcement is NOT suspended offline. C is wrong because audit and notify actions also continue offline — not just blocks. B is wrong because going offline does not trigger MDE device isolation; offline is a normal state for an enrolled device.

questions.stem: Endpoint DLP must block printing of Confidential labeled files to all printers EXCEPT the corporate print server. What should you configure?
options: A DLP policy with a Block all print action and an IP-address-based exception for the corporate printer
A Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Attack Surface Reduction rule excluding the corporate print server
A printer group for the authorized server, with a rule blocking all other printers
A SharePoint DLP policy preventing downloads of Confidential files before they reach the print spooler
questions.explanation: C is correct. Endpoint DLP has 'Printer groups' in global settings — you define groups by printer friendly name, IP range, or USB device ID, then reference those groups in DLP rules (e.g., 'block printing Confidential files to any printer NOT in the Corporate Printers group'). A is wrong because Endpoint DLP rule actions do not take an inline IP-exception field; the proper construct is a printer group. D is wrong because SharePoint DLP cannot control endpoint print events. B is wrong because ASR (Attack Surface Reduction) targets exploit and process behaviors, not data-loss print controls.

questions.stem: You need Endpoint DLP to restrict uploads of sensitive files to personal cloud storage (Google Drive, personal OneDrive) while allowing uploads to corporate SharePoint. What should you configure?
options: A sensitive service domain group in Endpoint DLP, referenced by DLP rules
A Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps session policy blocking uploads to non-corporate cloud storage URLs
A Microsoft Intune network isolation policy preventing access to non-corporate URLs from managed devices
A Web Content Filtering policy in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint blocking consumer storage sites
questions.explanation: A is correct. 'Sensitive service domain groups' in Endpoint DLP global settings let you categorize cloud-service URLs (corporate vs personal storage, approved vs unapproved). DLP rules then reference those groups to block, audit, or allow uploads to specific domain categories — providing granular control. D is wrong because Web Content Filtering in MDE blocks navigation entirely; it does not selectively manage uploads of sensitive content. B is wrong because the scenario specifies Endpoint DLP, not MDCA — and while MDCA session policies can also do this, sensitive service domain groups are the canonical Endpoint DLP mechanism. C is wrong because Intune network isolation is too coarse; it blocks all access, not just sensitive uploads.

questions.stem: A DLP policy must detect credit card numbers in Power BI semantic models and notify data stewards. Where should this DLP policy be configured?
options: Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps with Power BI connected via an API connector
Microsoft Purview auto-labeling policy targeting Power BI workspace content
Microsoft Purview portal — DLP policy with Power BI workspaces as the location
Power BI admin portal — Data protection settings for individual datasets
questions.explanation: C is correct. Microsoft Purview DLP has native Power BI support — when creating a DLP policy you can select 'Power BI workspaces' as a location and configure SIT conditions and notification/restriction actions against semantic models. A is wrong because MDCA can monitor Power BI but is not the native Purview DLP path. D is wrong because the Power BI admin portal manages tenant-wide settings (label enablement, sensitivity-label settings), not DLP rules. B is wrong because auto-labeling policies apply SENSITIVITY labels, not DLP actions.

questions.stem: You want a retention label to auto-apply to SharePoint documents that contain specific classification keywords in their text content. Which auto-apply condition should you configure?
options: Auto-apply using a trainable classifier trained on example documents
Auto-apply triggered by a SharePoint column default value in the document library
Auto-apply using a KQL keyword query that searches document content for the classification terms
Auto-apply using a named entity SIT for the classification identifiers
questions.explanation: C is correct. Auto-apply retention label policies support a KQL query condition that searches document content and indexed metadata. When documents match, the retention label applies automatically — no user action required. A (trainable classifier) is wrong here because classifiers detect content categories from training examples, not specific keyword lists; KQL is the right tool for explicit terms. D is wrong because named entity SITs are designed for entity classes (person names, addresses), not arbitrary classification keywords. B is wrong because library-column defaults trigger labeling only at the document-library level, not based on a search of document text.

questions.stem: A Teams DLP policy is active. Users frequently share files via cloud attachment links (SharePoint/OneDrive links in Teams chat). What must you enable in the DLP policy to inspect the actual linked file content?
options: Enable Scan cloud attachments in the Teams DLP policy
Add SharePoint Online and OneDrive as additional locations to the same DLP policy
Enable session monitoring in MDCA for all Teams file link interactions
Create a separate SharePoint DLP policy with the same SITs targeting the same files
questions.explanation: A is correct. Enabling 'Scan cloud attachments' in a Teams DLP policy tells the policy to inspect the content of SharePoint/OneDrive files shared as cloud links inside Teams chat — not just the message text. Without this setting, the rule sees only the chat message and misses sensitive content inside linked files. B is wrong because adding SharePoint/OneDrive as additional locations applies DLP to those workloads separately; it does not connect the Teams chat detection to the linked content. D is wrong for the same reason — a separate SharePoint DLP policy is a parallel pipeline, not an integration. C is wrong because MDCA session monitoring is not required for this scenario; Purview Teams DLP handles cloud-attachment scanning natively.

questions.stem: Insider Risk Management sequence detection generates an alert when which scenario occurs?
options: A user performs a specific series of activities in a defined order within a configurable time window
Multiple users in the same department exhibit similar risk indicators within the same time period
A single upload event exceeds the volume threshold defined in the IRM policy
A user daily activity volume exceeds their personal 30-day behavioral baseline by a statistically significant margin
questions.explanation: A is correct. Sequence detection in IRM looks for ORDERED chains of activities — for example download → rename → upload to personal cloud → external forward — within a configurable time window. Individual steps may be benign; the sequence implies intent. C describes a single-event threshold, not a sequence. D describes anomaly detection against a behavioral baseline — a different IRM signal. B describes coordinated multi-user behavior, which is not what sequence detection covers.

questions.stem: What does Insider Risk Management's cumulative exfiltration detection evaluate?
options: A user's 30-day exfiltration compared with org or peer norms
A single upload event against a fixed file-size threshold set in the policy
The total number of DLP matches across every user in a department
A user's activity against their own 7-day average, ignoring their peers
questions.explanation: Cumulative exfiltration detection looks at a user's exfiltration activity across all channels over the last 30 days and assigns risk when it exceeds organization or peer group norms. Peer groups come from the Microsoft Entra organization hierarchy, shared SharePoint access, and job titles, so a salesperson who emails customers often is compared with other salespeople. It isn't a single-event threshold, a personal 7-day baseline, or a DLP match count.

questions.stem: A user is designated as a Priority User in IRM global settings. What is the effect on IRM risk scoring for that user?
options: Priority users are automatically enrolled in all active IRM policies regardless of their department or role
Priority user activities are automatically escalated to the CISO dashboard without review
Priority users receive a higher insider risk score weighting for the same activities compared to standard users
Priority users are excluded from IRM monitoring to reduce false positive alerts
questions.explanation: C is correct. Designating a user as a Priority User in IRM boosts the risk-score weighting of their activities — their risk scores accumulate faster and they reach alert thresholds at lower activity volumes. This reflects the elevated business impact of activities by executives, privileged admins, or other high-stakes employees. A is wrong because designating a Priority User does not auto-enroll them in policies — they must still be in scope of a policy. D is wrong because Priority Users are MORE scrutinized, not excluded. B is wrong because there is no automatic CISO escalation pipeline — alerts follow the standard reviewer workflow.

questions.stem: What are IRM notice templates used for in the case management workflow?
options: Generating automated weekly compliance summary reports sent to the CISO
Notifying external regulators when a confirmed data breach requires regulatory disclosure
Sending standard notices, such as awareness reminders or warnings, to users
Automatically notifying affected users managers when an IRM alert fires
questions.explanation: C is correct. Notice templates store pre-defined communications (awareness reminders, caution letters, formal warnings) that an IRM investigator can send to a supervised user from within the case workflow. They are dispatched manually, when an investigator decides to. D is wrong because notice templates do not auto-fire to a user's manager when an alert triggers — alerts and notices are separate constructs. B is wrong because IRM does not generate external regulator notifications; breach disclosure is a separate process. A is wrong because IRM does not produce automated weekly CISO digests.

questions.stem: Which IRM indicator detects when users browse to websites categorized as risky or in a restricted domain list defined by the organization?
options: Cumulative exfiltration threshold indicator
Security policy violation indicator
Risky browsing indicator
Sensitive email forwarding indicator
questions.explanation: C is correct. The risky browsing indicators fire when monitored users visit websites considered malicious or risky, such as those associated with malware, pornography, or violence. They rely on IRM browser signal detection (built into Microsoft Edge, and through an extension for Chrome). A is a separate indicator (cumulative exfiltration threshold). B is the 'Security policy violation' indicator — endpoint controls being bypassed or disabled. D is the 'Sensitive email forwarding' indicator — a different signal entirely.

questions.stem: A compliance admin needs to identify all files deleted from a specific SharePoint site over the past 60 days using the unified audit log. Which audit operation should they filter on?
options: FileModified
FileAccessed
FileDeleted
FilePreviewed
questions.explanation: C (FileDeleted) is correct. The FileDeleted operation records when a user deletes a document from a site. Later deletions from the recycle bins are recorded separately, as FileDeletedFirstStageRecycleBin and FileDeletedSecondStageRecycleBin. B (FileAccessed) is wrong — that logs reads/previews. D (FilePreviewed) is wrong — preview operations, not deletions. A (FileModified) is wrong — edits to file content or metadata.

questions.stem: MailItemsAccessed events are now captured with Audit (Standard). Which detail of these events still requires Audit (Premium) licensing for the user?
options: The identity of the user who accessed the mailbox items
The sensitivity label of the mail items that were accessed
The date and time when the mailbox items were accessed
The mailbox in which the accessed items are stored
questions.explanation: Microsoft expanded Audit (Standard) to include MailItemsAccessed, but the SensitivityLabel property on those events is an Audit (Premium) intelligent insight that requires the user to have an Audit (Premium) license, such as Microsoft 365 E5 or E5 Compliance. The timestamp, the user, and the mailbox are basic properties of every MailItemsAccessed record.

questions.stem: When you use the keyword list format in a content search (one keyword per row), what additional reporting does this provide compared to a single compound query?
options: Estimated eDiscovery processing costs broken down per individual keyword
Per-keyword match counts and location statistics for each individual search term
Confidence scores indicating how accurately each keyword matched the target content
A geographic heatmap showing where matching content is stored across sites and mailboxes
questions.explanation: B is correct. The keyword-list format (one keyword per row) produces per-keyword statistics — match counts and locations for each individual term. This helps refine searches by spotting which keywords are over- or under-performing. D is wrong because Content Search does not produce a geographic heatmap. C is wrong because keyword matches do not produce ML-style confidence scores — that is a SIT/classifier concept. A is wrong because Content Search does not estimate per-keyword processing costs.

questions.stem: Which information is displayed in the DSPM for AI dashboard in Microsoft Purview?
options: Label coverage, oversharing risk, and AI interaction activity
The internal model weights and system prompts used by Copilot
Number of AI model parameters and training dataset sources used by Microsoft 365 Copilot
Real-time token usage and per-user cost analytics for Microsoft 365 Copilot interactions
questions.explanation: A is correct. DSPM for AI shows three primary signal types: (1) sensitivity labels present on content accessed by Copilot, (2) oversharing risk — broadly accessible or unlabeled content being surfaced — and (3) AI interaction activity metrics. C is wrong because the dashboard does not expose model parameters or training data sources — those are Copilot internals, not customer data. D is wrong because token usage and per-user cost analytics live in admin/billing reports, not DSPM for AI. B is wrong because Copilot's internal model weights and system prompts aren't customer data and aren't exposed anywhere in Purview.

questions.stem: Why is investigating a DLP alert in Microsoft Defender XDR advantageous over reviewing it only in the Microsoft Purview portal?
options: Defender XDR automatically remediates DLP violations using machine learning-based response
Defender XDR provides per-file encryption status details not visible in the Purview DLP alert dashboard
Defender XDR processes and surfaces DLP alerts faster due to real-time streaming pipelines
Defender XDR correlates DLP alerts with identity, device, and email signals
questions.explanation: D is correct. Defender XDR ingests DLP alerts and correlates them with signals from Defender for Endpoint (device risk), Entra ID Protection (sign-in/identity risk), and Defender for Office 365 (email threats) into a single unified incident with cross-product context. The Purview portal shows DLP alerts in isolation. C is wrong — the differentiator is correlation, not raw alert speed. A is wrong because Defender XDR does not auto-remediate DLP violations with machine learning. B is wrong because per-file encryption status is not surfaced in either portal — this option is fabricated.

questions.stem: Employees in the trading division are sending regulatory non-compliant investment advice in Microsoft Teams. Which Microsoft Purview solution should you configure to detect and review these communications?
options: A Communication Compliance policy using a regulatory compliance template
An Insider Risk Management data leaks policy targeted at the trading division
An eDiscovery case with a Teams-location keyword search for regulatory terminology
A DLP policy targeting Teams messages for financial sensitive information types
questions.explanation: A is correct. Communication Compliance with the financial-regulatory communications template applies classifiers tuned to detect regulatory non-compliance language — insider-trading indicators, Reg FD violations, fiduciary conflicts, and inappropriate investment advice — in email and Teams messages. D is wrong because DLP detects sensitive DATA (credit cards, SSNs); it cannot infer whether advice is regulatory-compliant. B is wrong because IRM detects user RISK behaviors (downloads, exfiltration) — not message content compliance. C is wrong because eDiscovery searches existing content; it does not provide ongoing supervision or content classification.

questions.stem: The Legal and M&A Advisory teams must be prevented from communicating with each other in Microsoft Teams due to conflict of interest rules. Which Microsoft Purview feature enforces this?
options: Microsoft Purview Information Barriers configured between the two organizational segments
Microsoft Entra ID access packages restricting Teams membership for both groups
Sensitivity labels with restricted user-based access on shared Teams channels
Communication Compliance policies monitoring cross-team message content for conflict keywords
questions.explanation: A is correct. Information Barriers (IB) define organizational segments and prevent specified segments from communicating in Teams chat/channels, SharePoint sharing, and OneDrive sharing — explicitly designed for ethical walls between groups like Legal/M&A advisory and trading/research. C is wrong because sensitivity labels gate access to CONTENT, not communication between user populations. D is wrong because Communication Compliance MONITORS messages but does not prevent the communication itself. B is wrong because Entra ID access packages govern application/resource access, not interpersonal communication blocks.

questions.stem: A document in SharePoint has a manually applied Client Hold retention label. An auto-apply retention label policy targets the same site and runs. What happens to that document?
options: The auto-apply policy does not apply its label — the existing manually applied label is preserved
Both labels are applied — SharePoint supports multiple retention labels per item
The auto-apply policy replaces the manual label with its configured label
The auto-apply policy applies its label only if it has a higher priority number than the existing label
questions.explanation: A is correct. Once a retention label has been manually applied to a document, auto-apply retention label policies do NOT overwrite it. The manual label takes precedence — this protects deliberate human/compliance decisions from automated overrides. C is wrong because auto-apply does not replace manual labels. B is wrong because a SharePoint item carries exactly one retention label at a time; multiple retention labels per item are not supported. D is wrong because no priority-number comparison occurs — manual labels are simply preserved.

questions.stem: Once a document is labeled Client Matter — Regulatory Record, no user or compliance administrator can remove the label or modify the document.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Regulatory Record labels lock content permanently — no user, records manager, Compliance Administrator, or even Global Administrator can remove the label or modify the document. This permanent immutability is exactly what distinguishes Regulatory Records from Regular Records (which CAN be temporarily unlocked by an authorized admin). No would be wrong because it implies someone retains an unlock capability, which Regulatory Records explicitly do not allow.

questions.stem: A compliance administrator can unlock a document labeled Internal Documents (Regular Record type) to allow temporary editing.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Regular Record labels permit a records administrator to temporarily unlock the record, allow edits, and re-lock it. This admin-unlock capability is the defining contrast with Regulatory Records, which cannot be unlocked by any administrator. No would be wrong because it would conflate Regular Records with Regulatory Records.

questions.stem: If Preservation Lock is applied to the 7-year retention policy, a Global Administrator can extend the policy duration to 10 years.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Preservation Lock prohibits WEAKENING the policy: shortening the duration, removing locations from scope, or deleting the policy. It PERMITS changes that make retention MORE restrictive — extending duration or adding locations. Extending a 7-year policy to 10 years is a permitted operation. No would be wrong because extension is explicitly allowed under Preservation Lock.

questions.stem: Microsoft 365 Copilot will not surface a document encrypted with the Strictly Confidential label to attorneys not listed in the label permissions.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Microsoft 365 Copilot honors sensitivity label encryption — content protected with 'Assign permissions now' is only retrievable by users in the permission set, regardless of underlying SharePoint or OneDrive access permissions. Attorneys not listed in label permissions will not see the document in Copilot's grounding results. No would be wrong because it implies Copilot can bypass label encryption — it cannot.

questions.stem: When a user downgrades a document from Strictly Confidential to a lower-priority label, no justification is required as long as mandatory labeling is not enabled.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: No is correct. Label downgrade justification is a SEPARATE policy setting from mandatory labeling — the two are configured independently in the sensitivity label policy. If 'Require justification for downgrade or removal' is enabled, the user must provide a justification regardless of whether mandatory labeling is on. Yes would be wrong because it incorrectly couples two independent policy switches.

questions.stem: An auto-apply retention label policy targeting the Northwind SharePoint site will overwrite a manually applied Client Matter — Regulatory Record label on existing documents.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: No is correct. Auto-apply retention label policies do not overwrite manually applied retention labels by default — the existing manual label is preserved. On top of that, Regulatory Record labels are permanently immutable: no automated policy can remove or replace them. Yes would be wrong on both counts — both manual-label precedence and Regulatory immutability protect the label.

questions.stem: Adatum uploads scanned PDF lab reports to SharePoint. DLP policies must detect SSNs and compound codes in these scanned images, but detection is failing for PDF files. What must be enabled in Microsoft Purview first?
options: Enhanced PDF protection in sensitivity label encryption configuration
Document fingerprinting for PDF file formats
Optical character recognition (OCR) in Purview settings
Advanced classification scanning in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint
questions.explanation: C is correct. OCR (Optical Character Recognition) must be explicitly enabled in Microsoft Purview Information Protection settings before DLP and auto-labeling policies can read text out of scanned PDFs and image files. OCR is OFF by default. Once on, OCR extracts text from images during content scanning so SITs can match against the extracted text. D is wrong because 'Advanced classification scanning in MDE' is not the gating setting for image-based content classification in Purview — Purview OCR is. B is wrong because document fingerprinting matches structural template layout, not image-to-text conversion. A is wrong because 'Enhanced PDF protection' is not a real Purview setting and would not enable image OCR even if it existed.

questions.stem: Adatum needs to detect documents containing proprietary compound names that no built-in SIT recognizes. The names follow no consistent alphanumeric pattern and cannot be enumerated in a finite list. What should they build?
options: A trainable classifier trained on example compound documents
A custom regex SIT with a pattern matching the general structure of compound names
A keyword dictionary SIT listing all known compound names
An EDM classifier using a database table of all compound names
questions.explanation: A is correct. Trainable classifiers use machine learning to recognize content categories from training examples — ideal when content has no consistent pattern and cannot be enumerated. Because Adatum's compound names have no fixed alphanumeric pattern and the full list cannot be reliably enumerated, a classifier trained on documents containing compound-name content is the strongest match. B (regex SIT) is wrong because no consistent pattern exists to write a regex for. D (EDM) is wrong because EDM requires a finite, enumerable data table — and Adatum cannot enumerate all compound names. C (keyword dictionary SIT) is wrong because it requires listing all terms; the question states the names cannot be enumerated.

questions.stem: Adatum requires that the most sensitive trade secret documents be encrypted such that Microsoft, Azure, and any cloud provider cannot decrypt them — even under legal compulsion. What encryption technology meets this requirement?
options: Azure Rights Management with Bring Your Own Key (BYOK)
Advanced Message Encryption with custom branding and access control
Double Key Encryption (DKE)
Microsoft Purview Customer Key for M365 data at rest
questions.explanation: C (DKE) is correct. DKE uses two simultaneous encryption keys: one held in Azure RMS (Microsoft) and one held exclusively by the organization on infrastructure Microsoft does not operate. Both keys are required for decryption — Microsoft cannot decrypt DKE content alone, even under legal compulsion. A (Azure RMS with BYOK) is wrong because while the customer supplies the root, Microsoft still has operational access to the key in Azure. D (Customer Key) is wrong for the same reason — Microsoft has operational access to keys in Azure Key Vault. B (Advanced Message Encryption) is wrong because AME is for emails, not document-level encryption, and Microsoft retains operational access to AME keys.

questions.stem: External academic collaborators (B2B guests) need access to SharePoint documents labeled Confidential - Research. The label uses Assign permissions now encryption scoped to internal Adatum users only. Collaborators receive Access Denied errors. What should Adatum configure?
options: Remove the encryption from the Confidential - Research label for any document shared externally with guests
Create a sublabel Confidential - Research (External) that grants access to the collaborator email domains or specific guest accounts
Grant collaborators SharePoint Site Owner permissions to bypass sensitivity label encryption restrictions
Switch the label from Assign permissions now to Let users assign permissions for all externally shared documents
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Assign permissions now' grants access ONLY to the specific users, groups, or domains explicitly defined in the label. To extend access to external academic collaborators without dropping protection on internal use, create a sublabel of Confidential - Research that explicitly grants access to the collaborator email addresses or domains. This adds a targeted encrypted variant for external sharing while keeping the internal label intact. A is wrong because removing encryption defeats the purpose of the label and exposes content to anyone with the link. C is wrong because SharePoint Site Owner permissions do NOT bypass label encryption — encryption operates at the identity layer regardless of SharePoint role. D is wrong because 'Let users assign permissions' shifts the burden to senders and creates inconsistent protection — not a sustainable enterprise pattern.

questions.stem: How do named entity SITs (such as All Full Names or All Physical Addresses) differ from standard pattern-based SITs?
options: Named entity SITs use machine learning models; standard SITs use rules, regex patterns, and keyword lists
Named entity SITs use regular expressions; standard SITs use machine learning models
Named entity SITs only detect content in English; standard SITs support multiple languages
Named entity SITs require EDM for high-confidence matching; standard SITs are self-contained
questions.explanation: A is correct. Named entity SITs (All Full Names, All Physical Addresses, Medical Terms) use machine-learning models to detect real-world entities that vary significantly in format, language, and structure — traditional regex cannot reliably capture them. Standard pattern-based SITs use regex with supporting keyword lists, ideal for structured data like credit card numbers or SSNs. B reverses the technologies — that is the opposite of how the two SIT families work. C is wrong because named entity SITs cover multiple languages, not just English. D is wrong because named entity SITs do not require EDM corroboration; they are self-contained ML detectors.

questions.stem: When must you re-upload and re-hash the sensitive data table for an EDM classifier?
options: Every 90 days — EDM hashes expire automatically on a fixed schedule
Whenever the source records change and matches must stay current
Once per year during the annual data governance review period
Only when the EDM schema definition (column structure) changes
questions.explanation: B is correct. EDM hashes represent the data at a specific point in time. When the underlying database records change — new hires, account updates, departures — you must re-hash and re-upload the data table for EDM to reflect the current records. There is no automatic expiration; the customer chooses the refresh cadence based on data volatility. A is wrong because hashes do not expire on a fixed 90-day schedule. D is wrong because schema changes do require re-upload but record-level changes ALSO require it — schema isn't the only trigger. C is wrong because the cadence depends on how often data changes, not an annual governance review.

questions.stem: An EDM SIT has one primary element (SSN) and two supporting elements (Last Name, Date of Birth). Which condition produces a High confidence match?
options: The SSN primary element matches any record in the database regardless of supporting element presence
The SSN and both supporting elements match one record, in proximity
The SSN primary element matches the database exactly on its own
The SSN primary element matches AND at least one supporting element is present in the document
questions.explanation: B is correct. High-confidence EDM matching requires the primary element to match AND supporting elements to also be present in close proximity, all aligned to the SAME database record. This multi-field corroboration distinguishes legitimate records from coincidental pattern hits. C is wrong because matching the primary alone yields a lower confidence level. D is wrong because at least one supporting element doesn't necessarily mean both — and high confidence requires all configured supporting elements to align. A is wrong because the primary alone is not enough for high confidence.

questions.stem: During a trainable classifier testing phase, you review candidate items and mark some as Not a match. What does this labeling provide to the classifier?
options: A neutral sample that has no measurable impact on classifier accuracy
A negative sample teaching the classifier that this content does NOT belong to the target category
A false positive correction that permanently removes the item from the candidate pool
A positive sample confirming this content is a good example of the target category
questions.explanation: B is correct. During the testing phase, items marked 'Not a match' become negative samples that teach the classifier what the target category does NOT look like — improving its ability to distinguish target content from similar-but-different content. Both positive AND negative feedback improve accuracy. D is wrong because 'Not a match' is a negative sample, not a positive confirmation. A is wrong because negative samples do measurably affect classifier accuracy. C is wrong because marking an item does not 'remove it from the candidate pool' — it labels the item for training purposes.

questions.stem: An external user with a Microsoft account receives a document labeled with Assign permissions now encryption. The label grants access to Adatum internal users only. Can the external user open the document?
options: Yes — if the external user has guest status in Adatum Entra ID directory
No — Assign permissions now grants access ONLY to the specific users, groups, or domains defined in the label configuration
Yes — external users with valid Microsoft accounts can always access sensitivity label encrypted content
No — only users in the same Entra ID tenant can decrypt any sensitivity label encrypted content
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Assign permissions now' encryption grants access ONLY to users/groups/domains explicitly defined in the label configuration. External users not in those permissions cannot decrypt the content — regardless of whether they have a Microsoft account, guest status, or any SharePoint role. Encryption enforces access at the identity layer. C is wrong because a Microsoft account alone does not grant access to encrypted content. A is wrong because guest status in the directory does not bypass label permissions. D is wrong because cross-tenant access is possible when the label explicitly grants it — the limit is the label's permission list, not the tenant boundary.

questions.stem: Your organization used Azure Information Protection (AIP) with labels defined in the Azure portal. After migrating to Microsoft Purview Information Protection, where are sensitivity labels managed?
options: Microsoft Entra ID admin center — Data classification settings
Azure Portal — Information Protection blade (still active for legacy labels after migration)
Microsoft Purview portal — Information Protection — Sensitivity labels
Microsoft 365 admin center — Information governance policies
questions.explanation: C is correct. After migrating from Azure Information Protection (AIP) to Microsoft Purview Information Protection, all label management moves to the Microsoft Purview portal under Information Protection → Sensitivity labels. The Azure portal Information Protection blade is deprecated for new work. B is wrong because the Azure blade is no longer the management surface. A is wrong because Entra ID admin center does not manage sensitivity labels. D is wrong because the M365 admin center holds tenant-level settings but not label management.

questions.stem: When should you use Double Key Encryption (DKE) rather than standard sensitivity label encryption with Azure Rights Management?
options: When rules require that no cloud provider, including Microsoft, can read it
When you need to apply encryption retroactively to large volumes of existing documents at scale
When you need to encrypt emails sent to external recipients who do not use Outlook
When users need to access encrypted content from both Windows and macOS devices simultaneously
questions.explanation: A is correct. DKE is reserved for the most sensitive content where regulatory or contractual requirements forbid any cloud provider — including Microsoft — from ever accessing the plaintext. Standard sensitivity-label encryption uses Azure RMS, where Microsoft has operational key access. DKE adds a second organization-controlled key so no single party can decrypt. C is wrong because DKE is not designed for non-Outlook email encryption; OME is. B is wrong because DKE does not specialize in retroactive bulk encryption; auto-labeling does that. D is wrong because cross-platform access (Windows/macOS) is not what DKE addresses; standard label encryption already works across platforms.

questions.stem: What is the correct sequence to configure Adaptive Protection so that DLP policies can dynamically enforce controls based on a user's current insider risk level?
options: Create an adaptive scope in data lifecycle management, then reference it in both the IRM policy and DLP rule conditions
Configure the DLP policy first with the insider risk level condition, then enable Adaptive Protection in IRM settings
Enable Adaptive Protection in Compliance Manager, then link it to both IRM and DLP policies from a central dashboard
Enable Adaptive Protection in IRM global settings first; once active, add the insider risk level is condition to DLP policy rules
questions.explanation: D is correct. The required sequence is: (1) enable Adaptive Protection in IRM global settings — this activates risk-level assignment (Minor, Moderate, Elevated) for users in IRM policy scope; (2) once Adaptive Protection is running, the 'Insider risk level is' condition becomes available in DLP rules; (3) add the condition to DLP rules to apply tiered enforcement (e.g., Elevated = block, Moderate = block with override, Minor = audit). B is wrong because DLP cannot reference risk levels before Adaptive Protection is enabled. C is wrong because Compliance Manager does not configure Adaptive Protection. A is wrong because adaptive scopes target retention policy populations, not insider-risk-driven DLP enforcement.

questions.stem: A sensitivity label policy is scoped to the Legal department (50 users). A Finance employee who is NOT in the policy scope receives a Word document with a Confidential - Legal sensitivity label applied. What happens when the Finance employee opens the document?
options: Word blocks the Finance employee from opening the document — label policy scoping enforces content access control by department
Word opens it with the label shown, but they can't apply that label
Word prompts the Finance employee to select a label from their own policy before they can view the document
Word automatically adds Confidential - Legal to the Finance employee sensitivity bar when they interact with the labeled document
questions.explanation: B is correct. Sensitivity label policies control which labels are AVAILABLE for users to apply — not which labels users can open. The Finance employee can open and read the labeled document normally (assuming they have SharePoint/Exchange access and decryption rights). However, Confidential - Legal will not appear in their sensitivity bar because the publishing policy isn't scoped to them — they cannot apply it themselves. A is wrong because label policy scoping does not gate read access — encryption does. D is wrong because the label is not auto-added to the Finance user's bar via interaction. C is wrong because Word does not prompt them to select a label from their policy before viewing.

questions.stem: To implement Double Key Encryption (DKE), where must the organization host its second encryption key?
options: In a dedicated Microsoft Purview DKE vault provisioned through the compliance portal
On a service the organization hosts and controls, outside Microsoft's cloud
Distributed across both Azure and on-premises Active Directory using a hybrid key sharing configuration
In Azure Key Vault within the organization own Azure subscription, separate from Microsoft-managed key vaults
questions.explanation: B is correct. DKE requires the organization to host the second key on infrastructure that Microsoft does NOT control — typically on-premises servers, or a non-Microsoft private cloud. The organization key never lives in Azure. Microsoft holds one key in Azure RMS infrastructure; the customer holds the second on its own service. Both keys are required simultaneously for decryption, so neither party can decrypt alone. D is wrong because Azure Key Vault is Microsoft-operated infrastructure — hosting the second key in Azure defeats DKE's purpose. A is wrong because there is no 'Purview DKE vault' product. C is wrong because hybrid AD key sharing is not the DKE model; DKE is two distinct keys, not a single shared key.

questions.stem: Which built-in Microsoft Purview role allows a user to create and manage sensitivity labels and auto-labeling policies without granting access to DLP policy management, retention labels, eDiscovery cases, or Insider Risk Management?
options: Compliance Data Administrator
Information Protection Admins
Records Management
Security Reader
questions.explanation: B is correct. The Information Protection Admins role group is scoped to creating and managing sensitivity labels, label policies, auto-labeling policies, and protection settings (including DKE and Customer Key). It does NOT grant DLP, retention, eDiscovery, or IRM access — useful for least-privilege delegation of label administration. D (Security Reader) is wrong because it is read-only across security workloads. A (Compliance Data Administrator) is wrong because it is broader than label administration. C (Records Management) is wrong because it covers retention/records, not sensitivity labels.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes Activity Explorer from Content Explorer in Microsoft Purview?
options: Activity Explorer is specifically for IRM behavioral events; Content Explorer is exclusively for DLP rule matches
Content Explorer shows the current inventory of labeled items; Activity Explorer shows historical label and DLP activity events
Both tools display the same data but with different visualization formats for different audiences
Activity Explorer shows current labeled items; Content Explorer shows label change event history
questions.explanation: B is correct. Content Explorer = current INVENTORY of labeled and sensitive items across SharePoint, Exchange, and OneDrive — what is labeled right now (snapshot). Activity Explorer = HISTORY of labeling events, DLP rule matches, and endpoint activities — what changed, when, by whom (timeline). D reverses the two — Activity Explorer is history, not current state, and Content Explorer is inventory, not change history. C is wrong because the two tools surface fundamentally different data, not the same data in different formats. A is wrong because Activity Explorer covers labeling, DLP, and endpoint events broadly, and Content Explorer covers labeled content broadly — neither is restricted to IRM or DLP alone.

questions.stem: A user applies a Highly Confidential sensitivity label to a Word document and then saves it as PDF. What happens to the sensitivity label?
options: The label is lost during PDF conversion — PDF files do not support sensitivity labels
The PDF retains visual markings (header, watermark) but encryption is removed for compatibility
The user must manually re-apply the label to the PDF after saving it to the new format
The PDF inherits the sensitivity label and its protection settings from the Office application
questions.explanation: D is correct. When a labeled Office document is saved or exported as PDF directly from Word, Excel, or PowerPoint, the sensitivity label and its protection (encryption, content marking text) transfer to the PDF. The label persists across the format conversion when Office apps perform the conversion. A is wrong because PDFs DO support sensitivity labels. B is wrong because encryption is NOT dropped on export — both visual markings and encryption carry over. C is wrong because manual re-application is unnecessary; Office handles label propagation automatically.

questions.stem: A sensitivity label has content expiration set to 60 days. A user applies the label to a document on January 1. What happens on March 2 (day 61)?
options: The document enters disposition review and is sent to the designated reviewer queue
The document is permanently deleted from SharePoint by the expiration policy
The document can't be opened, even by users who had access
The label is automatically removed and the document becomes an unprotected file
questions.explanation: C is correct. Content expiration in a sensitivity label defines how long after protection is applied users can access the content. After expiration, the Azure Rights Management service returns an access-expired/access-denied response to attempted opens. The document itself is NOT deleted — it simply can no longer be decrypted. D is wrong because the label and its encryption stay on the file; it does not become unprotected. B is wrong because expiration does not delete content from SharePoint. A is wrong because content expiration is a sensitivity-label setting, not a disposition-review workflow.

questions.stem: How does a retention label configured as Retain for 5 years, then delete differ from one configured as Retain for 5 years only when the retention period expires?
options: Both labels require administrator action to delete content — neither label type auto-deletes without manual intervention
Retain-then-delete deletes content at period end; retain-only takes no action
Retain then delete triggers a mandatory disposition review at period end; Retain only does not require any review
Both labels automatically delete covered content when the 5-year period expires
questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Retain X years, then delete' actively schedules permanent deletion (or disposition review) at the end of the retention period. 'Retain only' protects content from user deletion DURING the period but takes NO delete action at the end — content survives and is simply no longer retention-protected. D is wrong precisely because Retain only does NOT delete at period end. C is wrong because Retain then delete does not require disposition review — it permanently deletes by default unless a review is configured. A is wrong because both labels operate without manual administrator action at period end (within their configurations).

questions.stem: Your organization requires that electronic records under FDA 21 CFR Part 11 cannot be altered or deleted for 10 years. Which retention label type satisfies this regulatory immutability requirement?
options: Regular record label with Preservation Lock applied to the parent retention policy
A sensitivity label with encryption preventing modification of document content
A default retention label with the delete action disabled for the 10-year period
Regulatory record label applied directly to the electronic records
questions.explanation: D is correct. Regulatory record labels provide permanent immutability — once applied, no user or administrator can remove the label, modify the document, or delete it before the retention period expires. This is exactly what FDA 21 CFR Part 11 immutability requirements call for. A is wrong because Regular records allow admin unlocking — Regulatory records do not. Preservation Lock prevents weakening the policy but does not make individual records permanently immutable. C is wrong because a 'delete-disabled' retention label is not an immutability primitive; users with appropriate permissions could still modify it. B is wrong because sensitivity-label encryption controls access — it does not provide record immutability.

questions.stem: You want all new documents uploaded to a specific SharePoint document library to automatically receive the Internal sensitivity label. What should you configure?
options: An auto-apply sensitivity label policy targeting that library using a KQL keyword query
