A default sensitivity label in the SharePoint document library settings
A DLP policy with an auto-labeling action triggered for new uploads to the library
A retention label with default labeling configured in the SharePoint site content type
questions.explanation: B is correct. SharePoint document libraries support a default sensitivity label configuration (in library settings). Any document uploaded that does not already carry a label receives the default at upload time — directly in the library settings, separate from Purview auto-labeling policies. A (auto-apply with KQL) is wrong because that approach uses Purview auto-labeling and a content query, not a per-library default. D is wrong because retention labels are a different label family — and content type defaults are a separate, less-flexible mechanism. C is wrong because DLP does not include an auto-labeling action; DLP enforces, while labeling is configured in Information Protection.

questions.stem: A DLP rule must block external email sharing of sensitive content EXCEPT when the recipient domain is in an approved partner list. Which DLP rule element should you use to implement this exception?
options: A sensitivity label exclusion in the DLP policy that marks approved-partner emails as exempt from detection
An exception (unless) condition in the DLP rule that excludes emails sent to approved partner domains
An OR operator between the external sharing condition and the approved domain exclusion condition
A separate higher-priority DLP rule that explicitly allows sharing to approved domains
questions.explanation: B is correct. DLP rules support exception ('unless') conditions that exclude specific scenarios from triggering the rule action. Adding 'except if recipient domain is in approved-partner-domains' means the block applies ONLY when external recipients are NOT on the approved list — no need for a second rule or complex OR logic. C is wrong because an OR condition would expand the rule's matches, not narrow them. D is wrong because DLP rules don't have an 'allow' action that cancels another rule's block — when several rules match, the most restrictive action is enforced, so an exception on the blocking rule is the intended construct. A is wrong because there is no 'sensitivity-label exclusion' marking partner emails as exempt in DLP — exceptions belong on rule conditions.

questions.stem: A user provides a business justification and overrides a DLP Block with override action. Where is this override event recorded for compliance review?
options: In an email notification automatically sent to the user manager upon override
In a SharePoint compliance list maintained by the information security team
In the user Entra ID audit log as a policy exception event
In Microsoft Purview DLP incident management and Activity Explorer
questions.explanation: D is correct. Block-with-override events — including the user-provided justification text, user identity, timestamp, and the involved content — are logged in the Purview DLP incident management dashboard and surfaced in Activity Explorer. Compliance admins can review override patterns to spot abuse or refine policy. C is wrong because the Entra ID audit log tracks identity events, not DLP justifications. A is wrong because manager emails are not the audit-of-record (and aren't sent by default). B is wrong because there is no built-in SharePoint compliance list for DLP overrides.

questions.stem: A DLP policy is in Test mode without policy tips. Which statement accurately describes its behavior?
options: No user policy tips are shown and no admin alerts are generated — the policy runs completely silently
Users see policy tips; blocking occurs on high-confidence matches only; admins receive alerts
No user policy tips are shown; DLP matches ARE reported in DLP activity reports for admin review; no blocking occurs
Users see policy tips; admins receive email alerts; no blocking or enforcement occurs
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Test mode without policy tips' (formerly TestWithoutNotifications) runs the DLP engine in evaluation-only mode: no user policy tips, no enforcement actions, but matches ARE recorded in DLP activity reports and Activity Explorer for admin review. This lets admins assess policy impact before enabling enforcement. D is wrong because policy tips are NOT shown in this mode. A is wrong because matches ARE reported even though the policy runs without user-facing tips — it is not entirely silent. B is wrong because no blocking occurs in test mode regardless of confidence.

questions.stem: A Windows device with Endpoint DLP enabled is connected to the corporate network. A user copies a sensitive file from a local drive to a mapped network drive. Can Endpoint DLP monitor this activity?
options: Yes — Endpoint DLP includes copy to network share as a monitorable and controllable activity
No — network drive activity requires a separate SharePoint DLP policy to detect the file movement
No — Endpoint DLP only monitors local disk operations, not network file share paths
Yes — but only if the network drive is within the same Active Directory domain as the device
questions.explanation: A is correct. Endpoint DLP monitors a range of file activities on Windows devices — including 'copy or move to network share.' This lets organizations detect and restrict sensitive files being moved from devices to file shares, a common exfiltration vector. The activity can be audited, warned on, or blocked per DLP rule. C is wrong because Endpoint DLP DOES monitor network-share copy operations. D is wrong because there is no AD-domain restriction on Endpoint DLP's network-share monitoring. B is wrong because SharePoint DLP is for SharePoint Online, not for network file shares.

questions.stem: You want a retention policy to dynamically include all Microsoft 365 users in the Legal department, automatically adding new hires and removing departures. Which adaptive scope type should you use?
options: Role scope — based on administrative roles assigned in Entra ID
Group scope — based on M365 Group membership or group attributes
User scope — based on Entra ID attributes like Department
Site scope — based on SharePoint site URL patterns
questions.explanation: C is correct. Adaptive scopes come in three flavors — User (targets user mailboxes/OneDrive based on Entra ID attributes like Department, Title, Country), Site (SharePoint sites based on site properties), and M365 Group (group mailboxes/SharePoint based on group attributes). A User scope with Department = Legal dynamically includes current and future Legal employees with no manual policy updates. D (Site) is wrong because the targeting unit is users in Legal, not specific SharePoint sites. B (Group) is wrong because the requirement is by department, not group membership. A (Role) is wrong because 'Role scope' targets Entra admin roles — and is not the right granularity for a department's worth of users.

questions.stem: A Microsoft Teams private channel has messages that must be retained for 5 years. Which retention policy location should you select?
options: SharePoint Online — the private channel connected SharePoint site
Microsoft Teams — private channel messages
Exchange Online — shared mailboxes (each private channel has its own mailbox)
Microsoft Teams — channel messages
questions.explanation: B is correct. Teams private channel messages have a dedicated retention location ('Teams private channel messages') separate from standard channel messages. Selecting 'Teams channel messages' does NOT cover private channels — they must be explicitly added. D is wrong because standard 'Teams channel messages' does not include private channels. C is wrong because while each private channel has its own connected mailbox, you do not target it via 'Exchange Online shared mailboxes' in retention — the dedicated private-channel location is the right path. A is wrong because the private-channel SharePoint site is a separate target for FILE retention, not message retention.

questions.stem: An eDiscovery hold is placed on a SharePoint site. A user deletes a document and then empties both recycle bins. Where is the document preserved?
options: Nowhere, because emptying the second-stage recycle bin removes it permanently
In the case's review set, which the hold populates automatically
In the site's Preservation Hold library, for as long as the hold applies
In the user's OneDrive recycle bin, for another 93 days
questions.explanation: While a site is on hold, SharePoint keeps a copy of content that's deleted or modified in the site's Preservation Hold library, which ordinary users can't purge. Emptying the recycle bins doesn't remove that copy. Holds don't add items to review sets — collections do — and OneDrive isn't involved for a SharePoint site's files.

questions.stem: Your organization stores sensitive research data in Azure Blob Storage containers. Can Microsoft Purview Content Search search this data for eDiscovery?
options: Yes — if the Azure storage account is registered in Microsoft Purview Data Map first
Yes — Content Search covers all Microsoft cloud storage including Azure infrastructure services
No — Content Search covers Microsoft 365 workloads, not Azure storage
Yes — when Azure Blob Storage is connected via a Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps API connector
questions.explanation: C is correct. Microsoft Purview Content Search (eDiscovery) covers only Microsoft 365 workloads — Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, OneDrive for Business, Teams, Viva Engage. Azure Blob Storage, Azure Data Lake, and other Azure infrastructure storage are NOT searchable through Content Search. B is wrong because Content Search is M365-scoped, not 'all Microsoft cloud storage.' A is wrong because registering Azure storage in Purview Data Map enables data governance discovery — not Content Search/eDiscovery. D is wrong because the MDCA API connector does not extend Content Search to Azure storage.

questions.stem: You turn on an auto-apply retention label policy. How long can it take before the label is applied to all matching existing content?
options: Up to 7 days
Up to 24 hours
About 15 minutes
Up to 90 days
questions.explanation: Auto-apply retention label policies can take up to seven days to apply labels to all existing content that matches. Running the policy in simulation mode first lets you check what it would label before turning it on.

questions.stem: Your tenant has Microsoft 365 E3 licenses only. How long are audit log records retained by default?
options: 1 year
90 days
30 days
180 days
questions.explanation: Audit (Standard) retains audit records for 180 days by default; Microsoft increased this from 90 days for records generated on or after October 17, 2023. Audit (Premium), included with E5, keeps Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Microsoft Entra ID records for 1 year by default, and a 10-year add-on license extends that further.

questions.stem: An admin creates a custom role group containing only the Compliance Search and Case Management roles. A member can run searches but gets a permission error when exporting results. What's missing?
options: The Global Administrator role in Microsoft Entra ID
A Microsoft 365 E5 Compliance license for the member
Site collection administrator rights on each searched site
The Export role in the custom role group
questions.explanation: Exporting search results requires the Export role. The built-in eDiscovery Manager role group includes it, but a custom role group with only Compliance Search and Case Management lets members search without exporting — a common separation of duties. Global Administrator, extra licensing, and site collection admin rights don't grant export.

questions.stem: How does a DLP alert differ from an IRM (Insider Risk Management) alert?
options: DLP alerts flag sensitive data matches; IRM alerts flag risky user behavior
DLP alerts are generated in real time; IRM alerts are generated only during nightly scheduled risk analysis
DLP alerts are shown to end users via policy tips; IRM alerts are visible only to administrators
DLP alerts can trigger only on email content; IRM alerts trigger on activities across all M365 workloads
questions.explanation: A is correct. DLP detects sensitive CONTENT — specific data types (credit cards, SSNs) in specific locations. IRM detects risky USER BEHAVIOR PATTERNS — chains of downloads, exfiltration activities, and policy violations analyzed by ML risk scoring. Both generate alerts, but for fundamentally different signal types. C is wrong because DLP policy tips and IRM admin alerts are surface-level differences, not the core distinction. B is wrong because both DLP and IRM can generate alerts in near-real-time; IRM is not limited to nightly batch. D is wrong because DLP covers Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, and endpoint; it is not email-only.

questions.stem: Which factors primarily determine a user insider risk score in IRM?
options: The volume, frequency, and type of indicator activities detected
The number of DLP policy violations attributed to the user in the previous 30 days only
The sensitivity labels on content the user has accessed in SharePoint and OneDrive
The user salary band, performance rating, and tenure at the organization
questions.explanation: A is correct. IRM risk scores are calculated from detected indicator activities (downloads, USB copies, email forwards, cloud uploads, sequences), the volume and frequency of those activities, and Priority User weighting if applicable. D is wrong because salary, performance rating, and tenure are not IRM inputs. B is wrong because IRM risk is broader than DLP violations alone — many indicators contribute. C is wrong because content access metadata (which sensitivity labels a user has seen) is not a direct risk-score input.

questions.stem: An insider risk reviewer must triage alerts, manage cases, and view the actual files involved in an alert using Content explorer, but must not change IRM policies or settings. Which role group fits?
options: Insider Risk Management Analysts
Insider Risk Management Auditors
Insider Risk Management Admins
Insider Risk Management Investigators
questions.explanation: Investigators can access alerts, cases, analytics, notice templates, and Content explorer for alerts. Analysts can work alerts and cases but can't view content in Content explorer. Admins configure settings and policies, which is more access than needed, and Auditors review IRM audit logs.

questions.stem: An IRM alert is reviewed and determined to be a false positive — the activity was legitimate business use. Which action should the IRM reviewer take?
options: Escalate the alert to the IRM Investigator role for mandatory secondary review
Leave the alert open — dismissed alerts must remain visible to prevent future recurrence
Dismiss the alert as a false positive to remove it from the active alert queue
Convert the alert to a full case and then close the case as resolved
questions.explanation: C is correct. Alerts confirmed as false positives or benign activity should be dismissed from the triage view — this removes them from the active queue while preserving them in the historical audit log. Alerts should be promoted to a case only when investigation and action are warranted. A is wrong because mandatory escalation for every dismissed alert would create unnecessary review work. D is wrong because converting a false positive into a case is excessive — dismiss is the correct path. B is wrong because dismissed alerts remain in the historical log for audit even after being removed from the active queue.

questions.stem: When configuring the HR connector to import employee departure data from an HR system's CSV file, which has extra columns and its own column names, what flexibility does the connector provide?
options: The CSV must exactly match Microsoft required column headers and date format — no customization is permitted
The CSV must be converted to JSON format before the HR Connector can process it
Only departure dates in MM/DD/YYYY format are accepted — all other formats must be pre-converted externally
The connector field mapping configuration allows you to map your CSV columns to the required Purview IRM fields
questions.explanation: D is correct. The HR Connector setup includes field mapping configuration — you specify which CSV column corresponds to each required field (employee email, resignation date, termination date, last working day). Extra columns can simply be left unmapped. Date values still need to use the format the connector documents. A is wrong because the CSV does not have to exactly match a fixed Microsoft template. B is wrong because the CSV does not need to be converted to JSON. C is wrong because the connector doesn't require a US-style MM/DD/YYYY date — it documents its own required date format.

questions.stem: Which audit capability requires Audit (Premium) rather than Audit (Standard)?
options: Searching the audit log in the Purview portal
Creating custom audit log retention policies
Exporting audit search results to a CSV file
Running the Search-UnifiedAuditLog cmdlet
questions.explanation: Audit log retention policies — retaining records by service, activity, or user for up to 1 year, or 10 years with the add-on — are an Audit (Premium) feature. Searching in the portal, exporting to CSV, and the Search-UnifiedAuditLog cmdlet are all part of Audit (Standard).

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT something DSPM for AI in Microsoft Purview is designed to show?
options: Which sensitivity labels are on content accessed by Microsoft 365 Copilot
Users and sites identified as oversharing content surfaced by Copilot
AI interactions, including prompts and responses captured by policy
Copilot license costs and billing forecasts for each department
questions.explanation: DSPM for AI is a data security tool: it shows label coverage on content AI apps access, oversharing risks, and AI interaction activity — including prompt and response text in Activity explorer when collection policies capture it. License costs and billing are managed in the Microsoft 365 admin center, not in Purview.

questions.stem: Who can review flagged communications in a Communication Compliance policy?
options: Any member of the Communication Compliance role group regardless of policy assignment
Only users explicitly designated as reviewers when the policy was created
Any member of the eDiscovery Manager role group assigned to the policy
Any member of the Compliance Administrator role group in the tenant
questions.explanation: B is correct. Communication Compliance policies have designated reviewers specified at policy creation time. Only users explicitly added as reviewers for that specific policy can access and review the flagged communications — protecting employee privacy by strictly scoping access. D is wrong because Compliance Administrators do not automatically gain review access to flagged content. C is wrong because eDiscovery Manager role does not unlock Communication Compliance review. A is wrong because the Communication Compliance role group has rights only when assigned to that specific policy.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager?
options: Enforcing DLP and retention policies across all Microsoft 365 workloads
Monitoring and alerting on insider risk behavioral activities using machine learning analytics
Providing a compliance score and guided improvement actions for compliance with regulations and standards
Managing sensitivity label configurations and deployment across the entire tenant
questions.explanation: C is correct. Compliance Manager helps organizations assess and improve compliance posture against regulations (GDPR, HIPAA, ISO 27001, NIST, etc.). It produces a compliance score based on implemented controls, maps Microsoft controls to regulatory requirements, and offers prioritized improvement actions. A is wrong because Compliance Manager does not enforce DLP/retention — those are dedicated policy solutions. B is wrong because IRM, not Compliance Manager, monitors insider-risk behaviors. D is wrong because sensitivity labels are managed in Information Protection, not Compliance Manager.

questions.stem: You run a Content Search scoped to a Microsoft 365 Group. Which content locations are included in the search?
options: Only the group connected SharePoint site
Only the group Exchange Online shared mailbox
The group mailbox, SharePoint site, AND each member personal OneDrive for Business
Both the group's mailbox and its connected SharePoint site
questions.explanation: D is correct. Content Search against a Microsoft 365 Group includes the group's Exchange Online shared mailbox (conversations, calendar) AND the group's connected SharePoint site (files, wiki, pages). Individual member personal mailboxes and OneDrive accounts are NOT automatically included in a group-scoped search. B is wrong because both the mailbox AND SharePoint site are in scope, not just the mailbox. A is wrong for the same reason — the mailbox is also in scope. C is wrong because personal OneDrive accounts of members are not part of a group-scoped search.

questions.stem: Which requirement means you need an eDiscovery case with holds, rather than just running a search?
options: Finding mailboxes that contain a specific keyword
Estimating how many items a query will return
Preserving content in place for a legal matter
Previewing a sample of items that match a query
questions.explanation: Searching, estimating results, and previewing a sample are all things a search does on its own. Preserving content so it can't be permanently deleted while a legal matter is pending requires a hold, and holds are created and managed within an eDiscovery case.

questions.stem: A complex litigation case involves 15 key individuals whose mailboxes, OneDrive accounts, and Teams content must all be preserved under legal hold and searched together as a structured investigation. Which Microsoft Purview solution supports managing these individuals as named custodians with mapped data sources?
options: Microsoft Purview eDiscovery Standard — apply individual holds to each mailbox and OneDrive manually
Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management — create a case and add the 15 users as supervised subjects
Microsoft Purview Content Search with a static location list covering all 15 users
Microsoft Purview eDiscovery Premium — custodian management with data source mapping and custodian-specific holds
questions.explanation: D is correct. eDiscovery Premium introduces custodian management — you define custodians (the key individuals), map each custodian's relevant data sources (mailbox, OneDrive, Teams, SharePoint), apply custodian-level holds in bulk, manage legal hold notifications, and track responses, all within a structured case workflow. C is wrong because Content Search lacks hold and custodian management. A is wrong because eDiscovery Standard requires manual per-location hold application without custodian-centric workflow. B is wrong because IRM is for insider-risk behavior monitoring, not litigation case management.

questions.stem: In Discover mode (Policy enforcement = Off), the scanner generates a report of files matching classification rules without applying labels or modifying any files.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Discover mode (Policy enforcement = Off) is read-only — the MPIP Scanner identifies and reports matches against configured rules without applying labels or modifying any files. This is the recommended first mode to validate results before enabling Enforce mode. No would be wrong because that would imply Discover mode modifies files, which contradicts its purpose.

questions.stem: A SQL Server instance is required for the MPIP Scanner to store its configuration database and scan job results.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. The MPIP Scanner requires a SQL Server instance (Standard or Express) to store its configuration database, scan job settings, and scan results. SQL must be installed and accessible before the scanner can be configured and registered with the Purview portal. No would be wrong because SQL is a hard prerequisite — the scanner cannot run without it.

questions.stem: The MPIP Scanner can apply sensitivity labels to files on on-premises network file shares when Policy enforcement is set to On (Enforce mode).
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. When Policy enforcement is set to On (Enforce mode), the MPIP Scanner applies sensitivity labels and protection settings to files on on-premises network file shares per the configured content scan job. In Discover mode it only reports; in Enforce mode it labels. No would be wrong because labeling is exactly what Enforce mode does.

questions.stem: The MPIP Scanner can label and apply protection to files in SharePoint Online document libraries.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: No is correct. The MPIP Scanner targets ON-PREMISES environments — Windows file servers, network shares, and SharePoint Server (on-premises). SharePoint Online is covered by Microsoft Purview cloud auto-labeling policies, NOT by the MPIP Scanner. These are separate, complementary solutions for different environments. Yes would be wrong because it conflates the on-prem scanner's scope with the cloud auto-labeling product.

questions.stem: When in Enforce mode, the MPIP Scanner can apply sensitivity labels that include encryption (protection) — not just visual markings.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. In Enforce mode, the MPIP Scanner applies the full configuration of the matched sensitivity label — including encryption (Rights Management protection), content marking text, and other settings. The scanner is not limited to visual markings. No would be wrong because the Scanner does apply encryption when the matched label is configured with it.

questions.stem: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint must be deployed on the scanner server for the MPIP Scanner to function.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: No is correct. The MPIP Scanner is a standalone agent communicating with the Purview portal via the Azure Information Protection service — it does NOT require Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on the scanner machine. MDE is required for Endpoint DLP on Windows clients, not for the MPIP Scanner. Yes would be wrong because it would invent a dependency that does not exist.

questions.stem: Litware wants to stop Microsoft 365 Copilot from using files labeled Highly Confidential in its responses, even for managers who can open those files. What should Litware configure?
options: A DLP policy for the Microsoft 365 Copilot location that excludes the label
A Conditional Access policy that blocks the Copilot app for managers
A retention label on the files that removes them from the search index
A container label that limits unmanaged devices to web-only access
questions.explanation: Microsoft Purview DLP can target the Microsoft 365 Copilot location and prevent Copilot from processing items with specified sensitivity labels, while users who have access can still open the files directly. Retention labels don't control indexing, blocking the Copilot app removes it entirely, and container labels govern site access rather than Copilot processing.

questions.stem: When a Litware employee account is deleted, their OneDrive contained project files covered by an active 5-year retention policy. What happens to the OneDrive content?
options: Content is immediately deleted with the user account
Content stays in the Preservation Hold Library for the full 5 years
Content is preserved for 30 days and then deleted per the standard account deletion process
Content is automatically transferred to the deleted employee manager OneDrive account
questions.explanation: B is correct. Retention policies survive account deletion. OneDrive content covered by an active retention policy is preserved in the Preservation Hold Library for the full policy duration, regardless of the user account being removed. A is wrong because retention policy explicitly prevents immediate deletion. C is wrong because the standard 30-day OneDrive retention applies only when no retention policy is in effect. D is wrong because Microsoft does not auto-transfer OneDrive content to the manager — that would require a separate offboarding step and is not driven by retention policy.

questions.stem: Litware CISO wants a dashboard showing which project documents Copilot is accessing, whether they are sensitivity labeled, and whether sensitive unlabeled content is being surfaced to Copilot users. Which solution provides this visibility?
options: Microsoft Entra ID audit logs filtered for Microsoft 365 Copilot service principal activity
Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management scoped to Copilot-enabled users
Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI
Microsoft Defender XDR — Advanced Hunting with CopilotInteraction event type queries
questions.explanation: C (DSPM for AI) is correct. Data Security Posture Management for AI is the purpose-built Purview solution for Copilot governance visibility — sensitivity label coverage on content accessed by Copilot, oversharing risk on broadly accessible/unlabeled content, and AI interaction activity metrics. D is wrong because Defender XDR Advanced Hunting can query CopilotInteraction audit events but does not provide the dashboard-level governance view that DSPM for AI does. B is wrong because IRM detects user RISK behaviors, not Copilot content exposure. A is wrong because Entra ID audit logs show sign-in/service activity, not Copilot content access or labeling exposure.

questions.stem: Litware must detect full names of EU residents in SharePoint documents to comply with GDPR data subject rights requests. Names include many European cultural variations. Which SIT provides the best detection?
options: A custom regex SIT with patterns matching common European name formats
A named entity SIT, All Full Names, using ML across name variations
A keyword list SIT populated with employee names extracted from the HR database
An EDM classifier mapping names to a GDPR data subject registry maintained in SQL
questions.explanation: B (All Full Names) is correct. It is a named entity SIT using machine learning to detect person names across European, Asian, Middle Eastern, and other naming conventions without relying on fixed patterns. Ideal for GDPR scenarios where name formats vary widely across EU member states. A is wrong because no general 'European name format' regex can capture the cultural variation — and named entity SITs were specifically built to solve this. C is wrong because a keyword list from HR captures only employees, not all EU residents in customer data. D is wrong because building an EDM classifier of every EU subject's name is operationally infeasible and unnecessary when a named entity SIT does the job.

questions.stem: A sensitivity label Confidential has its header text changed from CONFIDENTIAL to CONFIDENTIAL — LITWARE INC in the Purview portal. When does the updated header appear on a previously labeled document?
options: The next time a user opens and saves the document in an Office application
Within 1 hour — as the label policy synchronizes to all Office applications automatically
Only when the user manually removes and re-applies the label to the document
Immediately — as soon as the label configuration is saved in the Purview compliance portal
questions.explanation: A is correct. Visual-marking changes (headers, footers, watermarks) on sensitivity labels take effect the next time a user opens and re-saves a labeled document in an Office application. Previously saved files do not retroactively update — the document must be re-opened and saved in Office after the updated label policy has propagated to the client (typically within an hour). D is wrong because the change is not applied immediately to previously saved documents — only on next save. C is wrong because manual remove-and-re-apply is not required; a normal save is enough. B is wrong because policy synchronization within an hour delivers the new label DEFINITION to Office, but the document itself still needs to be saved to receive the updated markings.

questions.stem: A compliance officer needs to determine what percentage of SharePoint documents are currently labeled versus unlabeled across the entire tenant. Which Microsoft Purview tool provides this inventory?
options: Activity Explorer — shows labeling change events sorted by date
Microsoft Purview Audit — filter for SensitivityLabelApplied operations across the tenant
Content Explorer — a current inventory by label, SIT, and location
Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager — data classification control assessment
questions.explanation: C is correct. Content Explorer provides the current inventory of labeled and sensitive items across SharePoint, Exchange, and OneDrive — filtered by label, SIT, or location. You can view item counts per label and identify coverage gaps. A (Activity Explorer) is wrong because it shows the HISTORY of labeling events, not the current state. B (Audit) is wrong because audit captures discrete events; aggregating into a tenant-wide inventory is what Content Explorer is for. D (Compliance Manager) is wrong because Compliance Manager tracks regulatory control implementation, not current label inventory.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares the scope of the MPIP Scanner versus Microsoft Purview cloud auto-labeling policies?
options: The MPIP Scanner operates on Windows and macOS devices; cloud auto-labeling covers Linux servers and cloud storage
Cloud auto-labeling is a superset of MPIP Scanner — the Scanner is only needed for EDM classification, not for actual labeling
The Scanner covers on-premises shares; auto-labeling covers Exchange, SharePoint, and OneDrive
Both the MPIP Scanner and cloud auto-labeling policies can label content in SharePoint Online and on-premises file shares
questions.explanation: C is correct. MPIP Scanner targets on-premises Windows file shares and SharePoint Server (on-premises). Cloud auto-labeling policies target Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and OneDrive for Business (the Microsoft 365 cloud). The two are complementary; neither covers the other's scope. D is wrong because they have distinct, non-overlapping scopes — the Scanner doesn't touch SPO and auto-labeling doesn't touch on-prem shares. B is wrong because cloud auto-labeling cannot label on-premises content, and the Scanner is more than an EDM tool — it applies any configured sensitivity label. A is wrong because the Scanner is not a Windows/macOS client agent — it is a server-side service.

questions.stem: Your financial services organization needs to detect potentially non-compliant investment advice and conflicts of interest in employee email and Teams messages. Which Communication Compliance policy template is designed for this scenario?
options: Regulatory compliance — uses classifiers trained to detect financial regulatory language and potential policy violations
Custom policy — no built-in template covers financial regulatory compliance scenarios
Offensive language — uses classifiers to detect harassment, threats, and discriminatory content
Sensitive information — detects messages containing sensitive information types such as credit card numbers or SSNs
questions.explanation: A is correct. The Regulatory compliance template in Communication Compliance uses ML classifiers trained on financial-regulatory language — detecting potential insider-trading indicators, Reg FD violations, fiduciary conflicts, and inappropriate investment advice. Financial-services firms should use this template as a starting point. C (Offensive language) is wrong because it targets harassment/discrimination, not regulatory matters. D (Sensitive information) is wrong because it detects structured DATA types (SSNs, credit cards), not regulatory content. B is wrong because a built-in regulatory compliance template DOES exist — a custom policy isn't required as the starting point.

questions.stem: Litware needs a second OME branding configuration for the Legal department, in addition to the existing corporate OME branding. Which PowerShell cmdlet creates a NEW OME branding template?
options: Add-OMETemplate — appends branding elements to the existing default configuration
New-OMEConfiguration — creates a new additional OME branding configuration template
Set-OMEConfiguration — modifies the existing default template with new branding settings
New-TransportRule with -ApplyOMETemplate — creates both the template and transport rule simultaneously
questions.explanation: B (New-OMEConfiguration) is correct. Set-OMEConfiguration only modifies the existing default OME template. New-OMEConfiguration creates an entirely new, separate OME branding configuration; multiple OME configurations can coexist in a tenant and are referenced from transport rules via the -ApplyOMETemplate parameter. C (Set-OMEConfiguration) is wrong because Set modifies the default, not creates a new template. A (Add-OMETemplate) is wrong because no such cmdlet exists. D is wrong because New-TransportRule creates the rule but does not create OME templates — the template must already exist before the rule references it.

questions.stem: A Confidential sensitivity label includes a watermark configured in the label settings. A user prints a document with this label applied. Where does the watermark appear on the printed output?
options: The watermark appears only on printed output from Windows — macOS printing omits watermarks
The watermark appears only on screen — sensitivity label watermarks do not appear on printed output
The watermark appears only on the first page — subsequent pages require a separate label configuration
The watermark is embedded in the document rendering and appears on printed pages
questions.explanation: D is correct. Sensitivity-label watermarks are inserted as document content — they appear both on screen AND in printed output across platforms. They are rendered as part of the document, not as a DRM-style screen overlay. B is wrong because watermarks DO appear on print. A is wrong because watermarks render on macOS prints as well — they are not OS-specific. C is wrong because watermarks repeat across pages, not just the first.

questions.stem: Which content marking types can a sensitivity label apply to a document?
options: Watermark only — headers and footers are controlled by the document template settings
Header text, footer text, watermark text, and a digital signature stamp
Header text and watermark only — footer text is not supported as a content marking
Header text, footer text, and watermark text
questions.explanation: D is correct. Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels support exactly three content-marking types: header text (top of pages), footer text (bottom of pages), and watermark text (diagonal overlay on each page). B is wrong because sensitivity labels do not insert a digital signature stamp as a content marking — the markings are limited to three text-based types. A is wrong because headers AND footers ARE supported in addition to watermarks. C is wrong because footer text IS a supported marking type.

questions.stem: In a sensitive information type (SIT), what is the purpose of a supporting element?
options: It defines the data format that the primary element regex pattern must match
It links the SIT to an EDM schema for exact-data validation of the primary element
It adds corroborating evidence near the primary element, raising confidence
It specifies which users are authorized to view content matched by the SIT in DLP reports
questions.explanation: C is correct. Supporting elements in a SIT (keywords, additional regex patterns, proximity conditions) provide corroborating evidence — when found near a primary-element match, they raise the confidence level (e.g., from medium to high). Without supporting elements, the primary match still fires but at a lower confidence level. A is wrong because the primary element's regex is fixed in its own configuration — supporting elements do not define it. D is wrong because RBAC governs report access, not SIT internals. B is wrong because EDM schemas are a separate SIT type — supporting elements are general SIT corroboration mechanisms.

questions.stem: You configure a service-side auto-labeling policy for SharePoint Online. The target sensitivity label uses which encryption configuration type?
options: Both Let users assign and Assign permissions now label configurations are equally supported
Only labels with Assign permissions now — pre-defined permissions requiring no user interaction
Labels with no encryption only — service-side auto-labeling cannot apply any encrypted label
Only labels with Let users assign permissions — service-side cannot apply pre-set permission labels
questions.explanation: B is correct. Service-side (cloud-based) auto-labeling can only apply labels configured with 'Assign permissions now' — because those permissions are pre-defined in the label and require no user decision at apply time. 'Let users assign permissions' requires interactive user input in an Office application and cannot be applied by an automated service-side policy. D is wrong — it reverses the relationship. A is wrong because the two encryption types are NOT equally supported by service-side auto-labeling. C is wrong because service-side auto-labeling CAN apply encrypted labels, as long as the encryption is 'Assign permissions now' type.

questions.stem: A DLP rule reports a sensitive information type match at High confidence. What does High confidence indicate?
options: A reviewer has manually confirmed the match is a true positive
The primary pattern matched along with strong supporting evidence
The matched item has a sensitivity label applied that includes encryption
The item contains more than 100 instances of the information type
questions.explanation: A SIT defines patterns at different confidence levels. A High confidence pattern requires the primary element plus more corroborating evidence — such as keywords, a checksum, or supporting patterns nearby — so it produces fewer false positives than Medium or Low. Instance count is a separate rule setting, confidence isn't a manual review outcome, and labels don't affect SIT confidence.

questions.stem: An employee notifies HR of their resignation effective in three weeks. Your organization wants IRM to immediately begin monitoring this employee for bulk downloads, USB copies, and unusual external email forwards during the notice period. Which IRM policy type should you configure?
options: Offensive language in the workplace — detects policy violations in employee communications
Security policy violations — detects users circumventing device security controls or disabling protective software
Data theft by departing employees — triggered by departure signals from the HR Connector and monitors exfiltration risk indicators
Data leaks — general — detects sensitive content being shared broadly across the organization or externally
questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Data theft by departing employees' is the IRM policy template designed for this scenario. When combined with HR Connector signals about resignation/termination, it activates heightened risk scoring during the notice period — monitoring for bulk downloads, USB copies, cloud uploads, and external forwards that may indicate pre-departure exfiltration. B (Security policy violations) is wrong because it targets users disabling/circumventing endpoint controls — different signal type. D (Data leaks - general) is wrong because it covers broad sharing/exfiltration without the departure-specific risk weighting. A is wrong because it is a Communication Compliance scenario, not IRM.

questions.stem: A retention label is configured with retention period starting from When labeled. A user applies the label to a document on March 1, 2025. The document was originally created January 1, 2023. The retention period is 5 years. When does the retention period end?
options: January 1, 2028 — 5 years after the document creation date
March 1, 2025 — the label application date itself, as retention triggers immediately
January 1, 2025 — 5 years calculated retroactively from the creation date
March 1, 2030 — 5 years after the label application date
questions.explanation: D is correct. 'When labeled' starts the retention clock at the date and time the label is applied — not the creation or modification date. March 1, 2025 plus 5 years equals March 1, 2030. The January 1, 2023 creation date is irrelevant to a 'When labeled' policy. A is wrong because that uses creation date, which is a different retention-basis option. C is wrong because retroactive calculation is not how 'When labeled' works. B is wrong because retention does not expire on the day the label is applied — the clock starts then.

questions.stem: Litware is a multinational company. EU employee data must not be accessible to US-based eDiscovery managers. Which Microsoft Purview feature restricts eDiscovery search scope by organizational geography or division?
options: Information Barriers configured between EU and US organizational units
Microsoft data residency commitments in the standard GDPR data protection addendum
Microsoft Entra ID administrative units limiting the search scope
Microsoft Purview Compliance Boundaries for eDiscovery
questions.explanation: D is correct. Compliance Boundaries in Microsoft Purview eDiscovery restrict which content locations (mailboxes, SharePoint sites) an eDiscovery manager can search and hold. They are designed for organizations with multiple divisions, geographies, or subsidiaries that need eDiscovery segmentation — exactly Litware's EU vs US separation. A (Information Barriers) is wrong because IB restricts user communication, not eDiscovery search scope. C (Entra administrative units) is wrong because admin units scope Entra administrative actions, not eDiscovery scope. B is wrong because data residency commitments protect storage location but do not segment eDiscovery roles by geography.

questions.stem: What is a key advantage of using a Microsoft Purview DLP policy over an Exchange mail flow rule (transport rule) for protecting sensitive information?
options: DLP policies evaluate content in real time before queuing; mail flow rules evaluate content only after queuing
Mail flow rules cannot block messages; only DLP policies can enforce blocking actions on email
Mail flow rules cannot apply to messages sent within the same organization; DLP policies can
DLP policies apply SIT-based detection across Exchange, SharePoint, Teams, and endpoints; mail flow rules cover Exchange email only
questions.explanation: D is correct. DLP policies use SITs (and other condition types) to detect sensitive CONTENT across multiple workloads — Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, endpoint, Power BI. Mail flow rules apply only to Exchange email. For consistent, content-aware protection across workloads, DLP is the right tool. C is wrong because mail flow rules can match internal-to-internal messages. A is wrong because both technologies evaluate before final delivery — the differentiator is content awareness, not timing. B is wrong because mail flow rules CAN block messages (Reject the message); blocking is not exclusive to DLP.

questions.stem: Litware needs a custom SIT to detect any of 20,000 proprietary technology terms in documents. A keyword list in a SIT is limited to 2,048 terms. What SIT feature supports a list this large?
options: Keyword dictionary, holding up to about 1 MB of compressed terms
A trainable classifier seeded with documents containing the terms
Extended keyword list with dynamic lookup from a SharePoint list
An EDM SIT using a 20,000-row database table of proprietary terms
questions.explanation: A is correct. Keyword lists inside a SIT are capped at 2,048 terms, while keyword dictionaries can hold much larger term lists — up to about 1 MB (roughly 1,000,000 characters) of compressed terms across all dictionaries. For 20,000 technology terms, a keyword dictionary is the right choice. C is wrong because there is no 'dynamic SharePoint list lookup' SIT type. B is wrong because trainable classifiers learn content topics from examples — they are not the mechanism for matching a specific list of terms. D is wrong because EDM matches structured rows of data with primary/supporting fields — not arbitrary technology terms.

questions.stem: You want a DLP alert to be generated only when a single incident involves more than 50 sensitive items — to reduce alert fatigue from low-volume matches. Where should you configure this threshold?
options: In Compliance Manager — set an incident count threshold per compliance control
In the DLP policy's alert settings, with a 50-item threshold
In Microsoft Sentinel — create a custom analytics rule that filters DLP signals below the threshold
In the sensitivity label policy alert settings for the matching label
questions.explanation: B is correct. DLP alert configurations include threshold settings — you can specify the minimum match count before an alert is generated. Setting a 50-item threshold means lower-volume incidents are still logged in DLP activity reports but no admin alert fires, reducing noise. D is wrong because alert thresholds are configured on the DLP policy, not on sensitivity label policy alerts. C is wrong because Sentinel is out of scope for SC-401 — it would be an over-engineered solution to a Purview-native problem. A is wrong because Compliance Manager assesses regulatory implementation, not DLP alert volumes.

questions.stem: Adaptive Protection in IRM assigns users to insider risk levels. Which risk level triggers the most restrictive DLP enforcement actions when combined with a DLP policy?
options: Critical
Moderate
Minor
Elevated
questions.explanation: D (Elevated) is correct. Adaptive Protection assigns three risk levels: Minor (lowest), Moderate, and Elevated (highest). DLP policies using the 'Insider risk level is' condition can apply tiered enforcement — Elevated typically triggers the strictest action (block), Moderate often block-with-override, Minor audit-only. A (Critical) is wrong because 'Critical' is NOT a valid Adaptive Protection level. C (Minor) and B (Moderate) are wrong because Elevated is more restrictive than both.

questions.stem: A user permanently deletes an email from their Exchange Online mailbox (purges it from Deleted Items). Where is the item stored and for how long by default?
options: The item is permanently and immediately deleted when purged from Deleted Items
The item moves to the archive mailbox immediately and is retained indefinitely
The item is moved to the archive mailbox Recoverable Items and retained for 90 days
The item is moved to Recoverable Items — Deletions folder and retained for 14 days by default
questions.explanation: D is correct. When a user purges an item from Deleted Items (Shift+Delete or empties the folder), the item moves to the hidden Recoverable Items → Deletions subfolder for 14 days by default. Litigation holds, eDiscovery holds, or retention policies extend this period — potentially indefinitely — and make the items discoverable via Content Search. A is wrong because the item is NOT immediately and permanently deleted; it goes to Recoverable Items first. C is wrong because the archive mailbox is not the default landing spot — the user's mailbox Recoverable Items is. B is wrong because items do not automatically migrate to the archive immediately, and they are not retained indefinitely without a hold.

questions.stem: A retention policy is configured with Retain only action (no delete) for a 5-year period applied to Exchange Online mailboxes. What happens to emails after the 5-year retention period ends?
options: Emails are flagged for disposition review at the 5-year mark and held pending review decision
Emails are automatically deleted by the retention policy after the 5-year period expires
Emails are automatically moved to the archive mailbox after 5 years
Emails remain in the mailbox indefinitely — Retain only has no automatic delete component
questions.explanation: D is correct. 'Retain only' ensures content CANNOT be permanently deleted by users during the retention period — but it does NOT schedule deletion at period end. After the period expires, the retention protection lapses and content is simply no longer shielded by the policy. Compare with 'Retain X years, then delete,' which actively schedules disposition. B is wrong because Retain only does not auto-delete. C is wrong because Retain only does not move content to archive. A is wrong because Retain only does not trigger disposition review at period end — that requires Retain-then-delete with reviewers configured.

questions.stem: Where should a compliance administrator navigate in Microsoft Purview to create a custom audit log retention policy extending retention for specific operations to 3 years?
options: Microsoft 365 admin center — Settings — Security and privacy — Audit
Microsoft Purview portal — Audit — Audit retention policies
Microsoft Entra ID admin center — Monitoring — Audit logs — Retention configuration
Microsoft Purview portal — Data lifecycle management — Retention policies
questions.explanation: B is correct. Custom audit log retention policies are configured in the Microsoft Purview portal under Audit, then on the Retention policies tab. These are separate from data lifecycle retention policies. Audit retention policies specify which workload record types to retain, for how long, and for which users/activities. D is wrong because Data lifecycle management retention policies cover content retention (emails, files), not audit logs. A is wrong because the M365 admin center does not house audit retention policy configuration. C is wrong because Entra ID admin center handles Entra audit logs separately — not Microsoft Purview unified audit log retention.

questions.stem: A DLP alert fires for a user who also has a high-risk Entra ID sign-in alert and a suspicious process execution alert from Defender for Endpoint. In which portal are all three signals consolidated into a unified security incident automatically?
options: Microsoft Entra ID portal — Risk events — Identity protection
Microsoft Sentinel — Incidents (requires individual data connector configuration for each source)
Microsoft Defender XDR portal — Incidents queue
Microsoft Purview portal — DLP alert management dashboard
questions.explanation: C is correct. Microsoft Defender XDR automatically correlates related alerts from Microsoft Purview (DLP), Entra ID Protection (identity risk), and Defender for Endpoint (device alerts) into a single unified incident with a complete attack story. D is wrong because the Purview DLP dashboard surfaces DLP alerts only — no cross-product correlation. A is wrong because Entra ID portal handles identity-risk events but is not the consolidation point for DLP + endpoint signals. B is wrong because while Sentinel can do this, it requires manual data connector configuration per source — Defender XDR provides the correlation natively for first-party signals.

questions.stem: Adaptive Protection is enabled and a user is assigned an Elevated insider risk level. A DLP policy rule uses the condition Insider risk level is Elevated with a Block action. The user attempts to upload a file — which contains no sensitive information types — to a personal cloud storage domain. What happens?
options: The upload proceeds — the insider risk level condition is informational only and does not trigger enforcement without a matching sensitive information type
IRM blocks the upload directly — Adaptive Protection does not route enforcement through DLP policies
The upload is blocked only after a second violation in the same session — the first attempt generates a warning
The upload is blocked — the user Elevated insider risk level alone satisfies the DLP rule condition and triggers the block action
questions.explanation: D is correct. When Adaptive Protection is active, the DLP condition 'Insider risk level is' can trigger enforcement based on the user's behavioral risk level ALONE — a matching SIT is NOT required. If the user is Elevated and the DLP rule blocks for Elevated, the upload is blocked regardless of file content. This enables proactive behavior-based enforcement on high-risk users. A is wrong because the condition does enforce without a SIT match. C is wrong because there is no automatic two-strike warning behavior built into the condition. B is wrong because IRM itself does not directly block — IRM provides the risk-level signal that DLP enforces against.

questions.stem: The FileAccessed audit event in the unified audit log records which activity?
options: When a file in SharePoint or OneDrive is opened or previewed by a user
When a file in SharePoint is permanently deleted by a user
When a sensitivity label is applied to a file for the first time
When a file is checked out for exclusive editing by a user in SharePoint
questions.explanation: A is correct. FileAccessed is generated in the SharePoint and OneDrive audit log when a user opens or previews a file — capturing user identity, IP address, file name, file path, and site URL. B (file permanently deleted) is FileDeleted — different operation. C (sensitivity label applied) is SensitivityLabelApplied — different operation. D (file checked out) is CheckOut — different operation.

questions.stem: A compliance administrator wants to search unified audit logs for Teams meeting recording activity using PowerShell. Which command sequence is correct?
options: Connect-IPPSSession; then Search-UnifiedAuditLog -RecordType MicrosoftTeams
Connect-MgGraph; then Get-MgAuditLogSignIn -Filter recordType eq MicrosoftTeams
Connect-ExchangeOnline; then Search-UnifiedAuditLog -RecordType MicrosoftTeams
Connect-IPPSSession; then Get-ComplianceCase -RecordType MicrosoftTeams
questions.explanation: C is correct. Search-UnifiedAuditLog is an Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlet — it REQUIRES Connect-ExchangeOnline before it can run, even though it queries the unified audit log that spans all M365 workloads. The cmdlet lives in the Exchange Online module, NOT in the Security & Compliance (IPPSSession) module. This is one of the most frequently tested SC-401 exam traps. A is wrong because Connect-IPPSSession does not expose Search-UnifiedAuditLog. B is wrong because Microsoft Graph audit cmdlets do not include Search-UnifiedAuditLog and Get-MgAuditLogSignIn is for Entra sign-ins. D is wrong because Get-ComplianceCase manages eDiscovery cases — not audit log search.

questions.stem: An eDiscovery hold is placed on a user Exchange Online mailbox as part of an eDiscovery Standard case. The user then deletes several emails and empties their Deleted Items folder. What happens to those deleted emails?
options: The emails are permanently deleted — eDiscovery holds only prevent future deletion, not items deleted after the hold is placed
The deleted emails are automatically added to the eDiscovery case review set when the user deletes them
The emails are preserved in the mailbox Recoverable Items folder and remain discoverable via content search within the case
The hold fails for newly deleted items — Litigation Hold must be used instead for prospective mailbox preservation
questions.explanation: C is correct. When an eDiscovery hold is placed on a mailbox, items the user deletes are moved to Recoverable Items → DiscoveryHolds subfolder rather than being permanently purged. They remain searchable and discoverable via content search within the case — applying both retroactively and prospectively while the hold is active. A is wrong because eDiscovery holds preserve future deletions too, not just past content. B is wrong because items are not automatically added to a review set on deletion — they are preserved in DiscoveryHolds and discoverable on demand. D is wrong because eDiscovery holds work prospectively just like Litigation Hold; both technologies preserve future deletions.

questions.stem: SharePoint content is covered by two retention policies: Policy A deletes content after 1 year, and Policy B retains it for 5 years with no delete action. What happens to the content?
options: It's deleted after 1 year, because deletion takes precedence
It's kept forever, because the conflicting policies cancel out
Nothing happens until an admin resolves the conflict manually
It's retained until the 5-year period ends and then deleted
questions.explanation: Under the principles of retention, retention wins over deletion, so Policy A can't delete the content while Policy B still requires it to be kept. Once the 5-year retention period ends, nothing prevents deletion any more, and Policy A's delete action takes effect. Conflicts are resolved automatically.

questions.stem: A retention policy covers Microsoft Teams channel messages for 3 years. A user deletes a channel message. Where is the deleted message preserved?
options: In the deleting user Exchange Online Recoverable Items folder
In the team connected SharePoint Preservation Hold Library
In a hidden SubstrateHolds folder within the team Exchange Online group mailbox
In the eDiscovery case hold container within the Microsoft Purview portal
questions.explanation: C is correct. Teams channel messages are stored in the team's Exchange Online group mailbox. When a retention policy applies and a message is deleted, the message is moved to the hidden SubstrateHolds folder within Recoverable Items of the group mailbox. This hidden folder is not user-accessible but is discoverable through eDiscovery. B is wrong because the SharePoint Preservation Hold Library preserves files in the connected SharePoint site, not Teams chat messages. A is wrong because Teams channel messages are not retained in the deleting user's personal mailbox. D is wrong because the eDiscovery case hold container is the search/result space, not the underlying preservation location.

questions.stem: A compliance admin wants to run a content search that includes an inactive mailbox (belonging to a user whose account was deleted 6 months ago). Which parameter is required?
options: -SearchInactiveExchangeLocationsEnabled $true
-AllowNotFoundExchangeLocationsEnabled $true
-ExchangeLocation InactiveMailboxes
-IncludeInactiveMailboxes $true
questions.explanation: B is correct. When adding inactive mailboxes (or other Exchange locations that do not have an active user mailbox) to a content search via PowerShell, you must include -AllowNotFoundExchangeLocationsEnabled $true on New-ComplianceSearch or Set-ComplianceSearch. Without it, specifying an inactive mailbox SMTP address returns an error because Exchange cannot find an active mailbox at that address. A is wrong because there is no -SearchInactiveExchangeLocationsEnabled parameter. D is wrong because -IncludeInactiveMailboxes is not the correct switch. C is wrong because -ExchangeLocation InactiveMailboxes is not a valid syntax.

questions.stem: A Confidential sensitivity label adds the header CONFIDENTIAL — DO NOT DISTRIBUTE but has no encryption. Can a user delete the header text from the document?
options: No — markings are locked while the label is applied
Yes — markings are document text that the user can delete
No — only the label's owner can edit content markings
Yes — but deleting it removes the label from the document
questions.explanation: Content markings — headers, footers, and watermarks — are inserted into the document as text and aren't technically enforced. Without encryption, a user can delete the header, and the label stays applied. Labels don't have owners who control marking edits. For enforceable protection, configure encryption with the label.

questions.stem: For Microsoft Purview to capture Microsoft 365 Copilot interaction events in the unified audit log, what is required?
options: Unified audit logging must be enabled in the Microsoft Purview compliance portal
Microsoft 365 E5 Advanced Audit licensing is required for all Copilot event types
Microsoft Defender for Endpoint deployed on all devices used with Copilot
DSPM for AI must have an active policy configured before Copilot events are logged
questions.explanation: A is correct. Copilot interaction events (CopilotInteraction record type) are captured in the unified audit log when unified audit logging is enabled — which is on by default for most M365 tenants. Basic Copilot events are captured at the Standard Audit tier. C is wrong because MDE on all devices is unrelated to Copilot service-side audit logging. D is wrong because DSPM for AI is not a prerequisite for audit log capture — it consumes audit data but doesn't unlock it. B is wrong because E5 Advanced Audit is not required for basic Copilot interaction events (although Premium events would need it).

questions.stem: An auto-labeling policy is actively applying the Internal sensitivity label (no encryption) to Exchange emails. You update the Internal label to add Assign permissions now encryption. What happens to future emails matched by the policy?
options: The auto-labeling policy stops functioning until the admin re-enables it with the updated label settings
Future matched emails will have the updated Internal label applied — including the new encryption settings
The policy must be deleted and recreated referencing the updated label to use the new configuration
Future emails continue receiving the old Internal label configuration for 72 hours during the policy cache refresh
questions.explanation: B is correct. Auto-labeling policies reference labels by identity. When the underlying label configuration is updated (e.g., adding encryption), the policy automatically uses the new settings for new applications — no policy reconfiguration required. The encryption takes effect for emails newly matched after the label-change propagates. A is wrong because the policy does not stop functioning when the label is updated. D is wrong because there is no 72-hour cache window that uses the old configuration. C is wrong because policy deletion/recreation is unnecessary — references are by identity.

questions.stem: A compliance officer uses Content Explorer and sees that 18,432 SharePoint items currently carry the Strictly Confidential sensitivity label. What does this count represent?
options: The number of unique users who have ever applied the Strictly Confidential label
The number of times the Strictly Confidential label was applied or changed in the past 30 days
The number of SharePoint items that currently carry the Strictly Confidential sensitivity label
The number of DLP policy rule matches involving Strictly Confidential labeled items
questions.explanation: C is correct. Content Explorer shows the CURRENT inventory of labeled items — 18,432 SharePoint items currently carry the Strictly Confidential label. It is a snapshot of current state. B is wrong because Content Explorer is not a 30-day event count — that is what Activity Explorer surfaces. D is wrong because DLP rule match counts are surfaced in DLP reports and Activity Explorer, not Content Explorer. A is wrong because unique-applier counts are not what Content Explorer reports.

questions.stem: You want a Proprietary Research retention label to auto-apply to documents that resemble research reports, without relying on specific keywords or consistent content patterns. Which auto-apply trigger should you use?
options: Auto-apply triggered by event-based retention with a research completion event type
Auto-apply using a KQL keyword query searching for research-related terminology
Auto-apply using a sensitive information type matching research report patterns
Auto-apply using a trainable classifier trained on example research report documents
questions.explanation: D is correct. Trainable classifiers use ML to identify content based on training examples — ideal when content has variable structure and no consistent keyword or data pattern, like research reports that share a topic and style but not a fixed format. B (KQL) is wrong because no specific keyword set is reliable — research reports vary in terminology. C (SIT) is wrong because research reports lack a structured data pattern a SIT could match. A (event-based) is wrong because event-based retention starts the clock from an event but does not auto-apply to content based on content similarity.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a DLP alert and a DLP report in Microsoft Purview?
options: DLP alerts flag individual matches quickly; DLP reports show trends
DLP alerts cover Exchange Online only; DLP reports aggregate activity across all DLP-enabled workloads
DLP reports are available only with Microsoft 365 E5 licensing; DLP alerts require only E3
DLP alerts are generated per user; DLP reports are generated per content location
questions.explanation: A is correct. DLP alerts are near-real-time notifications about specific rule matches — providing incident-specific detail for investigation. DLP reports (in the Purview portal under Reports) provide aggregated historical views: trend charts, top matched rules, top content locations, and policy match volumes. Alerts are for incident response; reports are for trend analysis. D is wrong because alert vs report is not split by user vs location. C is wrong because both alerts and reports are available regardless of license tier (subject to feature licensing). B is wrong because DLP alerts and reports both cover all DLP-enabled workloads.

questions.stem: Information Barriers policies in Microsoft 365 restrict communication and collaboration in which workloads?
options: Microsoft Teams only, with no file-sharing coverage
Microsoft Teams and SharePoint Online, but not OneDrive
All Microsoft 365 workloads, including Power BI and Viva
Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, and OneDrive
questions.explanation: D is correct. Information Barriers enforce communication and collaboration restrictions in: Microsoft Teams (chat and channels), SharePoint Online (sharing), and OneDrive for Business (sharing). B is wrong because OneDrive IS supported. A is wrong because IB extends beyond Teams. C is wrong because IB does not directly enforce in Power BI, Dynamics 365, or Viva — those are not standard IB-enforced workloads.

questions.stem: Which role group must a user belong to in order to create and manage Communication Compliance policies in Microsoft Purview?
options: Information Protection Admin
eDiscovery Manager
Communication Compliance Admins
Records Management
questions.explanation: C is correct. Creating and managing Communication Compliance policies requires the Communication Compliance Admins role group (or a broader one, such as Compliance Administrator). B (eDiscovery Manager) is wrong because eDiscovery rights do not include CC policy creation. D (Records Management) is wrong because that role manages retention/records, not CC. A (Information Protection Admin) is wrong because that role manages sensitivity labels, not CC policies.

questions.stem: What is a key difference between Exchange Online Litigation Hold and a Microsoft Purview retention policy applied to Exchange mailboxes?
options: Litigation Hold preserves all mailbox content indefinitely regardless of age; retention policies require a defined time period
Litigation Hold is configured per individual mailbox; retention policies can target all mailboxes at scale with a single policy
Retention policies preserve content for eDiscovery; Litigation Hold preserves content only for legal proceedings
Only retention policies are searchable via Content Search; Litigation Hold content is not discoverable
questions.explanation: B is correct. Litigation Hold is configured per individual mailbox via Exchange Online PowerShell (Set-Mailbox -LitigationHoldEnabled $true) and applies only to that mailbox. Retention policies can target mailboxes at scale — all users, static-scope user lists, or dynamic adaptive scopes — with a single policy. Both preserve content for eDiscovery, but retention policies scale more efficiently. A is wrong because Litigation Hold and retention policies can both preserve content indefinitely or for a defined period — duration is configurable in both. C is wrong because both preserve content for eDiscovery — they are not differentiated by 'compliance vs litigation' purpose. D is wrong because both retention policies and Litigation Hold content are searchable via Content Search.

questions.stem: A Communication Compliance policy has 50 specific users in the supervised population. Two supervised users exchange messages with each other. Are those messages captured by the policy?
options: Only one message per conversation pair is sampled daily to limit captured volume
Messages between two supervised users are captured
Messages between supervised users in the same department are excluded by default
Only messages FROM supervised users TO non-supervised users are captured
questions.explanation: B is correct. Communication Compliance captures inbound, outbound, AND internal communications for supervised users. Messages exchanged between two supervised users are fully in scope — the policy captures the complete communication universe of supervised users. D is wrong because internal messages between supervised users ARE captured, not excluded. A is wrong because there is no daily one-message sampling — the policy captures messages per its conditions. C is wrong because same-department supervised users are NOT excluded by default.

questions.stem: A Compliance Manager assessment shows a score of 420/1000 for GDPR. What does this score primarily reflect?
options: The estimated dollar value of potential GDPR fines avoided through current compliance controls
The number of GDPR articles Litware is fully compliant with out of 1,000 regulatory articles
The weighted percentage of GDPR improvement actions that have been implemented and validated
The number of days since the last GDPR-related data breach was reported to the supervisory authority
questions.explanation: C is correct. Compliance Manager scores reflect the weighted percentage of improvement actions implemented and validated, mapped to the selected regulation. Each action carries a point value based on risk impact and control importance. A higher score means more controls are implemented. B is wrong because the score is not a count of articles complied with — it is action-implementation weighted. A is wrong because the score is not a financial fine estimate. D is wrong because the score does not reflect time since last breach.

questions.stem: Before activating a new auto-labeling policy for Exchange Online in production, what should you do first to validate the policy scope and accuracy?
options: Run the policy against the previous 90 days of email using the historical analysis setting
Enable the policy in simulation mode and review the matched items report before turning on enforcement
Configure a low instance count threshold and gradually raise it after initial deployment
Deploy the policy to a single pilot mailbox using a static scope before expanding
questions.explanation: B is correct. Auto-labeling policies include a simulation mode that runs against existing content and reports what WOULD be labeled — without applying any labels. Reviewing simulation results lets admins assess accuracy (false positives and false negatives), refine conditions, and only then enable enforcement. D (pilot mailbox with static scope) is wrong because static scoping doesn't show the policy's accuracy against the broader content set — simulation does. C (low instance count threshold) is wrong because that affects which items match, not whether the policy applies labels. A (historical 90-day analysis) is wrong because such a setting is not part of auto-labeling configuration — simulation mode is the right tool.

questions.stem: The Search-UnifiedAuditLog command requires Connect-ExchangeOnline to be run first before it executes successfully.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Search-UnifiedAuditLog is an Exchange Online PowerShell cmdlet — Connect-ExchangeOnline must be established before running it. Despite querying the unified audit log that spans all M365 workloads, the cmdlet belongs to the Exchange Online PowerShell module. Connect-IPPSSession does NOT give access to this cmdlet — a frequently tested SC-401 trap. No would be wrong because it implies a different connection works, which is incorrect.

questions.stem: The command as written retrieves audit events across ALL Microsoft 365 workloads within the specified date range.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: No is correct. The -RecordType SharePointFileOperation parameter limits results to SharePoint file operation events; -Operations FileAccessed further narrows to file-access events specifically. The command does NOT retrieve events across all workloads — it is scoped to SharePoint FileAccessed only. Yes would be wrong because it ignores the explicit -RecordType and -Operations filters.

questions.stem: With Microsoft 365 E5 licenses assigned, users' Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Microsoft Entra ID audit records are retained for 1 year by default, without any custom audit retention policy.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Audit (Premium), included with Microsoft 365 E5 and E5 Compliance, has a default policy that retains Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Microsoft Entra ID records for 1 year; other records keep the 180-day Standard default. Custom audit retention policies can extend this further, up to 10 years with the 10-Year Audit Retention add-on. No would be wrong because 180 days is the Audit (Standard) default, not the E5 default for these workloads.

questions.stem: The 5-year custom SharePoint retention policy takes precedence over the 90-day default org-wide policy for the same SharePoint content.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. When multiple retention policies apply to the same content, the longest retention period wins (retain longer beats dispose sooner). The explicit 5-year custom policy also takes precedence over the org-wide 90-day default policy — content will be retained for 5 years. No would be wrong because retention conflict rules favor the longer retention.

questions.stem: To extend audit retention to 10 years for specific users, assigning a Microsoft 365 E5 Compliance license is sufficient — no additional license is required.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: No is correct. E5 and E5 Compliance provide 1-year default audit retention. Extending audit retention to 10 years requires BOTH an E5 (or E5 Compliance) license AND the separate Microsoft Purview Audit (Premium) 10-Year Retention add-on license. E5 alone is not sufficient. Yes would be wrong because it omits the required add-on.

questions.stem: A user must have the Audit Logs role in Exchange Online or the Compliance Administrator role to run Search-UnifiedAuditLog successfully.
options: Yes
No
questions.explanation: Yes is correct. Running Search-UnifiedAuditLog requires the View-Only Audit Logs or Audit Logs role assigned in Exchange Online (or a higher role like Compliance Administrator or Global Administrator that includes these rights). Without the role, the cmdlet returns empty results or an access-denied error even after Connect-ExchangeOnline succeeds. No would be wrong because role assignment is required in addition to the connection.
